title: 2.37 Flow-generated sphere–plane shrinkers
text: 45B364E949D5 (Hoffman–Martin–White sphere–plane family) Write $d_1=\sqrt{2\pi /e}$ and $d_2=4/e$. For every integer $g\geq 1$ and every fixed \[  1+d_2<\delta <1+d_1,  \] Hoffman–Martin–White construct a smooth embedded shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ of genus $g$ with $\lambda (\Sigma _ g)<\delta $. They produce it as a tangent shrinker of an intrinsically flowing compact surface in $S^2\times \mathbb R$; the tangent shrinker itself is Euclidean. It satisfies $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, with homothetic flow $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g$ for $t<0$. No explicit parametrization is known from this construction. This is a connected, orientable, complete, properly embedded surface of dimension two and codimension one. It contains the union $Q_ g$ of $g+1$ horizontal lines through the origin at angles $j\pi /(g+1)$, and $\Sigma _ g\cap \{ z=0\} =Q_ g$. In particular it is noncompact. Its complement of the horizontal plane has genus zero. The symmetry group $G_ g$ used here is generated by reflection in vertical planes at angles $(2j+1)\pi /(2(g+1))$, rotations about the vertical axis through $2\pi /(g+1)$, and half-turns about the lines in $Q_ g$. This is the Costa–Hoffman–Meeks symmetry group specified in Section 5. For all sufficiently large $g$, $\Sigma _ g$ has exactly one asymptotically conical end. For small $g$, the theorem does not specify an exact number of ends. For a fixed admissible $\delta $, as $g\to \infty $ the surfaces converge to $\{ z=0\} \cup S^2(2)$, smoothly with multiplicity one away from the equatorial intersection circle. The normalized Gaussian area equals entropy and obeys \[  F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ g)=\lambda (\Sigma _ g)<\delta <1+\sqrt{2\pi /e}<3.  \] The choice of $\delta $ is part of the existence statement; it does not assign an exact entropy to a fixed uniquely determined member. No identification with the Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz min-max examples or the Kapouleas–Kleene–Moller and Nguyen gluing examples is proved. The shared topology and limiting configuration do not establish that they coincide or are distinct. See [ HMW2026 ] , version 3: Section 5 (PDF pp. 16–17), Theorems 40–42 (pp. 26–31), Section 9 (p. 40), and Lemma 64 (pp. 45–46). The source uses $\leq \delta $ in Theorem 40; the strict bound above is its refined choice in Theorem 41. Figures 1 and 5 (PDF pp. 3 and 26) show numerical simulations credited to Francisco Torralbo and Mario Schulz. Our interactive picture is an original topology schematic informed by those figures and the sphere–disk surgery in Figure 6 (p. 27): a connected surface, a cutaway exposing its central sheet and lower cap, the exact horizontal trace $Q_ g$, and the separate sphere–plane limit. title: 2.38 Flow-generated three-ended shrinkers
text: 5CED6ED3B586 (Hoffman–Martin–White three-ended family) For every sufficiently large integer $g$, Hoffman–Martin–White construct a smooth embedded shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ with genus $2g$ and exactly three ends. It has the normalization and smooth evolution \[  \vec H=-X^\perp /2,\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ g,\quad t<0.  \] The construction obtains the surface as a multiplicity-one tangent shrinker of a flow whose initial surface is compact and embedded in $S^2\times \mathbb R$ with its product metric. The shrinker lives in the Euclidean tangent space. There is no explicit parametrization. It is a connected, orientable, complete, proper noncompact surface of dimension two and codimension one. Its topology is a closed genus-$2g$ surface with three punctures; the three ends are annular and asymptotically conical. It has the group $G_ g$ and the union of lines $Q_ g$ specified in Example 2.37 . In particular, $\Sigma _ g\cap \{ z=0\} =Q_ g$ and $\Sigma _ g\setminus \{ z=0\} $ has genus zero. These are the symmetries of the genus-$g$ Costa–Hoffman–Meeks minimal surface, but the shrinker has genus $2g$. As $g\to \infty $, the surfaces converge to the horizontal plane with multiplicity three. After passage to a subsequence, convergence is smooth away from one circle in that plane. The circle is part of the limiting analysis, not an independently prescribed radius. The entropy has a bound $\lambda (\Sigma _ g)\leq \Lambda <\infty $ independent of $g$, and $F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ g)=\lambda (\Sigma _ g)$. The paper does not specify a numerical value of $\Lambda $ in this theorem. This entry therefore does not assert $\lambda <3$ or an exact entropy limit. For each small $g$ the preceding construction produces a shrinker with genus $g$ or $2g$ and a uniform entropy bound; the assertions of genus $2g$ and three ends require $g$ sufficiently large. The paper's genus-two picture is explicitly conjectural and is not a numerical approximation. No uniqueness or identification with Shao–Zou's tripling construction is proved. See [ HMW2026 ] , version 3: Theorem 43 (PDF p. 31), Theorem 55 and Conjecture 56 (p. 38), Theorem 59 (p. 39), Proposition 62 and Lemma 64 (pp. 45–46). Its cutaway exposes the neck interiors, and its plan relates the necks to $Q_ g$. The separate limit view shows a single plane with multiplicity three. Neck sizes, end slopes, and the displayed circle radius are illustrative; no shrinker equation or mean curvature flow has been computed, and the displayed small values of $g$ do not assert three-ended existence. 5CED6ED3B586 (Hoffman–Martin–White three-ended family) For every sufficiently large integer $g$, Hoffman–Martin–White construct a smooth embedded shrinker $\Sigma _ g\subset \mathbb R^3$ with genus $2g$ and exactly three ends. title: 2.27 Ketover shrinkers with Platonic symmetry
text: [ Ketover2016 ] , Theorem 0.1, constructs five families by equivariant Gaussian min-max. The compact doubled solids used in the sweepout describe the genus and symmetry of the construction; compactness of the limiting shrinker is not proved. AE0CC89EB3E2 There are smooth connected embedded self-shrinking surfaces $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^3$ with the following pairs of genus and rotational symmetry group: \[  (g,G)=(3,T_{12}),\quad (5,O_{24}),\quad (7,O_{24}), \quad (11,I_{60}),\quad (19,I_{60}).  \] Here the subscripts give the orders of the tetrahedral, octahedral, and icosahedral rotation groups. The normalization is $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. No explicit parametrization is supplied. The sweepout joins two spherical sheets by one neck for each face of a tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, or icosahedron, respectively. The numbers of necks are $4,6,8,12,20$; the first neck connects the components, so the genus is one less than this number. This is a construction description, not an exact metric model. The min-max limit is multiplicity one. It is complete and proper, has no boundary, and retains the stated genus and symmetry. The construction controls the genus but does not determine compactness, the number of ends, or end asymptotics. In particular, a compact picture suggested by numerical work must not be used to assign zero ends to these proved examples. The proof gives a useful strict Gaussian-area bound: \[  \frac4e < F_{0,1}(\Sigma )=\lambda (\Sigma )<\frac8e.  \] For the doubled cube, the first equivariant width is $4/e$, the second is strictly below twice the first by Lemma 2.4, and the equality of the two widths is excluded in Remark 2.7. Remark 2.5 gives the same construction for the other four symmetry types. These are bounds, not computed entropy values. No uniqueness or stability classification is asserted. The two-parameter equivariant construction alone does not give an index bound for unrestricted variations. Later constructions with similar symmetries need not be different surfaces, and no identification is assumed here. The illustration shows the neck counts and symmetry of the sweepout, not a numerical solution or a proof of compactness of the limit. text: The Gaussian-width construction of [ SunWangZhou2024 ] produces shrinkers whose entropy is unbounded, in contrast with the uniform upper bounds for several gluing and low-parameter min-max families. 0177A2718D72 (Sun–Wang–Zhou Gaussian-width shrinkers) For every $2\leq n\leq 6$ there is a sequence of smooth, connected, embedded self-shrinking hypersurfaces $\Sigma _ k^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$. They are normalized by $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, with associated smooth flows $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma _ k$ for $t<0$. The construction is variational and does not give explicit parametrizations. Each shrinker is complete, proper, boundaryless, and has finite entropy. The construction is a multiplicity-one limit of free-boundary min-max hypersurfaces in exhausting balls with metrics approaching the Gaussian metric. The final shrinker has no free boundary. Write $G_ n=(4\pi )^{-1}e^{-|x|^2/(2n)}g_{\mathrm{Euc}}$ and let $\omega _ k(\mathbb R^{n+1},G_ n)$ be its Gaussian $k$-width, defined by exhaustion. Then \[  F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ k)=\lambda (\Sigma _ k) =\omega _ k(\mathbb R^{n+1},G_ n),\qquad \lambda (\Sigma _ k)\asymp k^{1/(n+1)}.  \] The growth statement means comparison up to positive constants depending on $n$, and in particular $\lambda (\Sigma _ k)\to \infty $. It is not a closed formula for an individual width or a plotted list of computed values. The unbounded entropies ensure infinitely many different examples, without requiring consecutive widths to be strictly different. The Gaussian Morse index for compactly supported normal variations satisfies $\mathrm{index}(\Sigma _ k)\leq k$. This is an upper bound, not an equality or an entropy-stability claim. The theorem does not specify a genus, a number of ends, end asymptotics, compactness, or a symmetry group for each member. In dimension two the genus is therefore left unrecorded in the property browser, rather than inferred from the min-max parameter. In every dimension $n\geq 2$ and for every $\Lambda >0$, there is a smooth embedded shrinker with $\Lambda <\lambda (\Sigma )<\infty $ and finite Gaussian index. For $n\geq 7$ this follows by taking a lower-dimensional example and a Euclidean product. For example, $\Sigma ^6\times \mathbb R^{n-6}\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ has the same entropy as $\Sigma ^6$, and Theorem 5.3 preserves finiteness of index under each line product. These higher-dimensional product examples are noncompact; this extension does not assert the $n$-dimensional Gaussian-width growth law above beyond $n=6$. Sources: [ SunWangZhou2024 ] , Theorem 1.6 and Corollary 1.7, arXiv version 1, PDF p. 4; Definition 5.1 and the proof of Theorem 1.6, pp. 39–42; Definition 5.2, p. 40; Theorem 5.3 and its proof, pp. 42–44. title: 2.33 Chu–Sun genus-one shrinkers below the shrinking doughnut
search_title: Chu–Sun genus-one shrinkers below the shrinking doughnut
section: 2.33 Chu–Sun genus-one shrinkers below the shrinking doughnut
text: The flow construction in [ ChuSun2025 ] gives an embedded genus-one shrinker with strictly less entropy than the Drugan–Nguyen shrinking doughnut. It does not identify the resulting surface with any particular previously constructed example. AE7721D6799F (Chu–Sun lower-entropy genus-one shrinkers) Let $\mathcal T\subset \mathbb R^3$ be the rotationally symmetric compact genus-one shrinker constructed by Drugan–Nguyen (Example 2.28 ). There is a smooth embedded genus-one shrinker $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^3$ satisfying \[  F_{0,1}(\Sigma )=\lambda (\Sigma ) <\lambda (\mathcal T)<2.  \] It has dimension two and codimension one, is normalized by $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and yields the smooth self-similar flow $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. The surface is a multiplicity-one tangent-flow model at a genus-one singularity of an ancient level-set flow which is asymptotic, after rescaling as $t\to -\infty $, to $\mathcal T$. The ancient flow is allowed to pass through cylindrical and spherical singularities before the genus-one singularity. Thus the theorem does not assert that this is the first singularity of a smooth ancient flow. The resulting shrinker is complete, proper, and boundaryless. Its compactness, end count, end asymptotics, and symmetry are not determined by this existence statement. No explicit parametrization, exact entropy value, or numerical shape is supplied. Strictly smaller entropy rules out congruence with the chosen shrinking doughnut $\mathcal T$. It does not prove that $\Sigma $ differs from the Buzano–Nguyen–Schulz genus-one example. Remark 1.5 discusses that example and its numerical evidence, without proving the identification. It also does not identify $\mathcal T$ with Angenent's shooting torus. For a shrinker minimizing entropy among all embedded genus-one shrinkers, Theorem 1.4 gives a further alternative: it is noncompact or has Gaussian Morse index exactly $5$. This statement applies to an entropy minimizer, not to every shrinker obtained by the interpolation construction. No uniqueness is asserted. Sources: [ ChuSun2025 ] , Theorems 1.4 and 1.6, Remark 1.5 and Corollary 1.7, arXiv version 3, PDF pp. 3–4; proofs in Sections 5.2–5.5, pp. 33–34. The diagram records the flow construction and strict entropy drop; the final genus-one shrinker is left abstract because its compactness and ends are not specified. title: 2.42 An embedded self-shrinking Möbius bundle (Lee–Mu-Tao Wang, 2007)

section: 2.42 An embedded self-shrinking Möbius bundle (Lee–Mu-Tao Wang, 2007)
text: This example is a surface in $\mathbb C^2=\mathbb R^4$, of codimension two. CC2E5DD6BD78 (An embedded nonorientable shrinker) Let $M=(\mathbb S^1\times \mathbb R)/((\theta ,r)\sim (\theta +\pi ,-r))$ and set \[  X([\theta ,r])=(e^{2i\theta }\cosh r,\sqrt2 e^{-i\theta }\sinh r).  \] This is an exact parametrization with $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$; its ancient flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, X(M)$, $t<0$. Lee–Wang constructed the surface, up to a unitary change of coordinates, in [ LeeWang2009 ] , Section 2.2. The quotient map is an embedding; the map on $\mathbb S^1\times \mathbb R$ is a double cover, not an embedding. The surface is Lagrangian, Hamiltonian stationary, noncompact, and asymptotic to a Schoen–Wolfson $(2,1)$ cone. Its topology is the open Mobius line bundle, with one end and one crosscap. Orientable surface genus does not apply. The identity $|X|^2=1+3\sinh ^2r$ proves properness, and the induced metric \[  g=(\sinh ^2r+2\cosh ^2r)(2\, d\theta ^2+dr^2)  \] proves completeness. The diagonal circle action has weights $(2,-1)$. For this single-covered embedding, [ BraxtonLeeZhu2026 ] , Theorem 1.2 and Section 7, prove $F$-stability under arbitrary normal variations modulo translations and dilation. This does not establish nonlinear stability or realization as a generic singularity. Remark 7.4 gives \[  F_{0,1}(M)=\lambda (M)=\frac{\sqrt2 e^{1/8}}8 \left[K_0(3/8)+3K_1(3/8)\right],\qquad K_ j(z)=\int _0^\infty e^{-z\cosh v}\cosh (jv)\, dv.  \] The illustration projects the exact four-dimensional parametrization; projected crossings are not self-intersections of $M$. title: 2.43 Compact periodic Lagrangian quadric shrinkers
text: These are the compact periodic solutions in the Joyce–Lee–Tsui construction. 98593B70A49E (Periodic quadric shrinkers) Fix $n\geq 2$, $a_ j>0$, $\alpha =-1/2$, and put $Q(u)=\prod _{j=1}^ n(a_ j+u)$ and $\phi =\sum _ j\phi _ j$. Solve \[  u'=2\sqrt{Q(u)}\cos (\phi -\theta ),\qquad \phi _ j'=-\frac{\sqrt{Q(u)}\sin (\phi -\theta )}{a_ j+u},\qquad \theta '=-\tfrac 12\sqrt{Q(u)}\sin (\phi -\theta ).  \] Require $a_ j+u>0$ and $A=\sqrt{Q(u)}e^{-u/4}\sin (\phi -\theta )>0$. Choose nonconstant periodic data for which all phase increments over a period of $u$ are rational multiples of $\pi $. A common period $T$ then closes all $w_ j(s)=\sqrt{a_ j+u(s)}e^{i\phi _ j(s)}$. The immersion is \[  X(x,s)=(x_1w_1(s),\ldots ,x_ nw_ n(s)),\qquad (x,s)\in \mathbb S^{n-1}\times (\mathbb R/T\mathbb Z).  \] Theorems A, B, E(a)(ii), and F of [ JoyceLeeTsui2010 ] establish these ODE solutions and a dense set of closing initial data. They satisfy $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, and $\sqrt{-t}\, X$, $t<0$, is their mean curvature flow. The parameter manifold is compact, hence the immersion is complete and proper. It has dimension and codimension $n$, no ends, and topology $\mathbb S^{n-1}\times \mathbb S^1$; for $n=2$ it is a torus. Coordinate reflections are symmetries. Embeddedness, uniqueness, and stability are not inferred from the immersion theorem. The drawing is a construction diagram, not a numerically closed solution. The constant-radius subcase, including familiar overlapping examples, is excluded here. 98593B70A49E (Periodic quadric shrinkers) Fix $n\geq 2$, $a_ j>0$, $\alpha =-1/2$, and put $Q(u)=\prod _{j=1}^ n(a_ j+u)$ and $\phi =\sum _ j\phi _ j$. title: 2.50 Lee–Wang embedded quadric shrinkers
text: 0EB941FB0D2B (An embedded mixed-sign quadric family) Let $n\geq 3$, $n/2<k<n$, and $S=2k-n>0$. Put \[  Q_+=\left\{ x\in \mathbb R^ n:\sum _{j\leq k}x_ j^2-\sum _{j>k}x_ j^2=2S\right\} ,\qquad X(x,s)=(e^{is}x_1,\ldots ,e^{is}x_ k,e^{-is}x_{k+1},\ldots ,e^{-is}x_ n).  \] The domain is the mapping torus \[  (Q_+\times \mathbb R)/((x,s)\sim (-x,s+\pi )).  \] This exact map gives a complete proper embedded Lagrangian of dimension and codimension $n$ in $\mathbb C^ n$, with $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$. Its flow is $L_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X(Q_+\times \mathbb R)$ for $t<0$. These are the unit-weight cases of [ LeeWang2010 ] , Propositions 2.1–2.2: the weights are $k$ copies of $1$ and $n-k$ copies of $-1$. The fiber $Q_+$ is $S^{k-1}\times \mathbb R^{n-k}$. The antipodal gluing is part of the topology; a product with $S^1$ cannot in general replace this mapping torus. The full manifold is connected, noncompact, and has one end. When $n-k=1$ the gluing exchanges the two fiber ends; otherwise the fiber already has one end. It is orientable exactly when $n$ is even. The $n=3$, $k=2$ case is a nonorientable three-manifold, not a surface with a genus. The $SO(k)\times SO(n-k)$ action and the indicated circle action preserve the image. The Lagrangian angle is $Ss+\pi /2$ locally; it is harmonic, so the example is Hamiltonian stationary, although it is not stationary under MCF. It is asymptotic to the corresponding quadric cone. Properness follows directly from $|X|=|x|$ on the mapping torus. Its polynomial volume growth gives finite entropy, equal to centered Gaussian area in this normalized shrinker setting; no numerical value or stability theorem is asserted here. The figure uses the exact $n=3$, $k=2$ case, as explained below. The companion expander is Example 4.18 . For the illustrated weights $(1,1,-1)$, put $r_ t(u)=\sqrt{u^2-2t}$. At $t<0$ the complete flow has the explicit coordinates \[  F_ t(\theta ,u,s)=\bigl (r_ t(u)\cos \theta \, e^{is}, r_ t(u)\sin \theta \, e^{is},u e^{-is}\bigr ), \qquad \theta \in \mathbb R/(2\pi \mathbb Z),\quad u\in \mathbb R,\quad s\in \mathbb R.  \] The circle coordinate obeys $(\theta ,u,s+\pi )\sim (\theta +\pi ,-u,s)$. Fixing $s=0$ gives $x_1^2+x_2^2-x_3^2=-2t$ and waist radius $\sqrt{-2t}$. The four views use one spatial scale and the fixed ambient crop $|F_ t|\leq 3.6$. Thus the shrinking waist approaches the cone while the noncompact ends remain visible. The cut edges are display boundaries. The phase leaves are two-dimensional slices of the full flow, and are not themselves surface mean curvature flows in $\mathbb R^3$. The circle-action view projects a selected phase leaf and sampled circle orbits by \[  P(z_1,z_2,z_3)=\left(\operatorname {Re}z_1, \frac{\operatorname {Re}z_2+\operatorname {Im}z_1}{\sqrt2}, \frac{\operatorname {Re}z_3+\operatorname {Im}z_2}{\sqrt2}\right).  \] Changing $s$ changes a spatial coordinate, not the time. Crossings in this projection need not be self-intersections in $\mathbb R^6$. The optional positive-time views use the same quadric equation, with $x_3=\pm \sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2+2t}$. These two real sheets belong to the connected companion expander after circle gluing. The $t=0$ cone is singular; Theorem 1.1 and Section 3 of [ LeeWang2010 ] give the Brakke continuation through it without mass loss, rather than a smooth flow across zero. 0EB941FB0D2B (An embedded mixed-sign quadric family) Let $n\geq 3$, $n/2<k<n$, and $S=2k-n>0$. title: 2.14 Chopp cubical shrinker candidate
text:
Chopp's level-set computations produce five new shrinker candidates in [ Chopp1994 ] . These entries describe numerical evidence, not existence theorems. The paper also recovers the Angenent torus of Example 2.13 . 04E9A0B8F725 (Numerical genus-five cube) The cubical candidate is a two-dimensional hypersurface in $\mathbb R^3$, with the topology of a closed orientable surface of genus five and cubical symmetry. Chopp starts with the boundary of a ball bored along the three coordinate axes. The connected central cavity has six openings; this is not a genus-three solid with three disjoint tunnels. The algorithm evolves a family of level sets, selects a level using a geometric ratio, and dilates to maintain a chosen volume. It gives an approximation, with no closed parametrization or exact implicit equation for the shrinker. The target equation and associated flow, in our convention, are \[  H= rac{\langle X,
u angle }{2},\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma ,\qquad -\infty <t<0.  \] Chopp's equation (3.1) instead uses $H=\langle X,
u angle /(2T)$ for an unrescaled surface $S$; the corresponding normalized surface would be $\Sigma =T^{-1/2}S$. His constant-volume display is not automatically the slice at $t=-1$. The intended surface is smooth, compact, embedded and without boundary; if such a surface exists it is complete and proper and has no ends. The computation does not establish this existence statement. The reported self-similarity diagnostic is $E=0.01869$, and subsequent ordinary MCF approximately preserves the computed shape. This is a finite-grid check, not a certified error bound. No uniqueness, stability spectrum, Gaussian area or entropy value is established for this particular candidate. title: 2.15 Chopp octahedral shrinker candidate
text: 5D3FB6DFEE3F (Numerical genus-seven octahedron) Chopp computes a closed genus-seven shrinker candidate in $\mathbb R^3$ by starting with a sphere bored in the eight directions $(\pm 1,\pm 1,\pm 1)$. There are four drilling axes and eight openings into the central cavity. The candidate has octahedral symmetry, dimension two and codimension one; its intended topology is a closed orientable surface of genus seven. The construction is numerical level-set evolution with dilation and level selection. It supplies neither a closed formula nor a proof of an exact solution. In normalized coordinates the target is $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$, with the proposed flow $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. The conversion from the paper's scale is described in Example 2.14 . title: 2.16 Chopp punctured-torus saddle candidate

title: 2.17 Chopp two-handled cone candidate

title: 2.18 Numerical four-handled cone shrinker candidate (Chopp, 1994)
text: F576920EB05F (The numerical Angenent–Ilmanen–Chopp surface) This is Chopp's numerical genus-three, two-ended shrinker candidate in $\mathbb R^3$. It is a surface of dimension two and codimension one, with intended topology a genus-three orientable surface minus two points. The four connecting necks do not give genus four. With its axis taken to be $x_1$, the symmetry group is $\mathbb Z_2\times D_4$, where $D_4$ has eight elements and acts on the transverse plane. The starting geometry is a cylinder with two transverse holes bored through its axis. Level selection balances radial and longitudinal neck pinches. Dilation then exposes a candidate whose two ends appear smoothly asymptotic to a nonrotational double cone $C$. The intended surface is smooth, embedded, complete, proper and without boundary, but its existence and asymptotics are numerical assertions in the cited papers. There is no closed formula. The normalization is \[  \vec H=-\frac{X^\perp }{2},\qquad M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma \quad (t<0),\qquad M_0=C.  \] Here the last equality describes the proposed singular trace, not a smooth slice. Chopp's displayed mesh requires a further dilation to obtain $\Sigma =M_{-1}$. The 1994 paper reports $E=0.0505$ and minimum cone opening about $1.2627$ radians. The 1995 paper reports approximately $1.263$ radians ($72.3$ degrees). These are numerical estimates without certified error bounds. The reported opening exceeds the numerically estimated critical rotational-expander aperture $66.04$ degrees. The barrier argument in the 1995 paper then predicts two distinct smooth self-expanding continuations for $t>0$ and fattening of the level-set flow. Its Main Result is explicitly conditional on Assertion 1 and verification of the numerics; it is not an unconditional existence proof for this particular genus-three surface. The level-set flow itself is unique as a set-valued flow; “nonuniqueness” here concerns distinct thin continuations inside it. Sources: [ Chopp1994 ] , Section 4.6, pp. 12–13, Figures 26–28; [ AIC95 ] , Section 1 and Assertion 1, pp. 1940–1944, Section 3, pp. 1953–1955, and the conditional Main Result in Section 4, p. 1956. No uniqueness, stability spectrum, Gaussian area or entropy value is established for the numerical shrinker. The double-cone expander results are recorded in Examples 4.5 and 4.6 . The rigorous Ilmanen–White family is separate (Example 2.34 ); its theorem does not identify a member with this computed mesh. The rotatable picture is a genus-three topology schematic with four necks and two ends. It neither solves the shrinker equation nor verifies fattening. Chopp's related compact four-handled dumbbell in Section 4.5, Figure 24, failed his self-similarity test ($E=0.584$) and is not a sixth shrinker candidate. Semiregular polyhedra and a trefoil are future-work proposals in Section 5, not constructions established there. section: 3.1 The grim reaper and its cylinders
text: 3B1939BC4D74 For unit upward translation, an exact parametrization in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=(x,y,-\log \cos x+t),\qquad |x|<\pi /2,\quad y\in \mathbb R^{n-1},\quad t\in \mathbb R.  \] For $n=1$ omit $y$. More generally the planar curve of speed $c>0$ has height $-c^{-1}\log \cos (cx)+ct$, on $|x|<\pi /(2c)$. The curve and all its Euclidean products are complete, properly embedded, noncompact, and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. Their motion is eternal. At unit speed the curve has curvature magnitude $\cos x$ and total curvature $\pi $. Its two ends have the vertical asymptotes $x=\pm \pi /2$. The product is invariant under translations in its $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ factor. For $n\geq 2$ its second fundamental form has rank one; in $\mathbb R^3$ its Gauss curvature is zero, so it is not strictly convex. As a translating graph it is stable for compactly supported variations of the translator weighted area. This is weighted stability, not a claim about stability for unweighted Euclidean area. The supplied notes [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Example 1.6, PDF page 4, use downward translation; the displayed surface is its reflection in a horizontal plane. Graphical weighted minimality is discussed in [ HIMWGraphical18 ] , Section 2, PDF page 5. 3B1939BC4D74 For unit upward translation, an exact parametrization in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=(x,y,-\log \cos x+t),\qquad |x|<\pi /2,\quad y\in \mathbb R^{n-1},\quad t\in \mathbb R.  \] For $n=1$ omit $y$. title: 3.8 Tilted grim-reaper cylinders
text: 56A3E33A9D04 Let $a\in \mathbb R$ and $A=1+a^2$. An exact unit-speed upward translator in $\mathbb R^3$ is \[  X(x,y,t)=\left(x,y,-A\log \cos (x/\sqrt A)+ay+t\right),\quad |x|<\frac\pi 2\sqrt A,\quad y,t\in \mathbb R.  \] This is a complete, properly embedded noncompact surface diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^2$. It has zero Gauss curvature and is invariant under translation in the direction $(0,1,a)$. Its horizontal graph domain is a strip of width $\pi \sqrt{1+a^2}$. The case $a=0$ is the ordinary grim-reaper cylinder. The underlying surface is a rotation and dilation of that cylinder. At a fixed width greater than $\pi $, the two signs of $a$ give the two opposite tilts. Translation in a tangent invariant direction does not change the evolving image. Products with Euclidean factors give higher-dimensional translators. Graphical weighted stability holds, as in the preceding example. See [ HIMWGraphical18 ] , equation (1.4), PDF page 3, with exchanged horizontal coordinates and reflected vertical direction. These cylinders must be distinguished from the strictly convex $\Delta $-wings on strips of the same width. 56A3E33A9D04 Let $a\in \mathbb R$ and $A=1+a^2$. title: 3.2 The rotational bowl translator
text: ECF360A3D482 For each $n\geq 2$, the bowl is the entire graph $z=f(r)$, $r=|x|$ in $\mathbb R^ n$, moving by $z\mapsto z+t$. Its radial profile is specified by the regular ODE \[  \frac{f''}{1+(f')^2}+\frac{n-1}{r}f'=1,\qquad f(0)=f'(0)=0,\qquad f''(0)=1/n.  \] This is an ODE characterization, not an elementary closed formula. The bowl is complete, properly embedded, strictly convex, rotationally invariant, and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. For $n\geq 2$ it has one topological end and gives an eternal flow. Up to a vertical additive constant, its height has asymptotic expansion \[  f(r)=\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}-\log r+C+O(r^{-1})\quad (r\to \infty ).  \] A paraboloid is only a leading approximation, not the exact translator. It is unique among entire rotationally invariant translating graphs, up to translation. In $\mathbb R^3$ it is the only complete entire translating graph, up to the natural rigid motions and normalization. In $\mathbb R^3$, Brendle–Choi's theorem characterizes its flow among noncompact, strictly convex, noncollapsed ancient flows, up to scaling and ambient isometries. These are the hypotheses of the cited classification. Graphical weighted stability holds. The stronger dynamical stability theorem of Clutterbuck–Schnürer–Schulze concerns continuous graphical initial data whose height difference from the bowl tends to zero at spatial infinity; the resulting height difference tends uniformly to zero as time tends to infinity. The supplied notes [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Section 4 and Theorem 4.1, PDF pages 10–11, describe the construction and classification. The original ODE and asymptotic analysis is [ CSS07 ] , Section 2, Lemmas 2.1–2.2; its Theorem 1.1 gives the stated dynamical stability. The ancient classification is [ BrendleChoi19 ] , Theorem 1.1, printed page 36 (PDF page 2). The entropy is $\lambda (\mathrm{Bowl}^ n)=\lambda (S^{n-1}(\sqrt{2(n-1)}))$, in particular $\sqrt{2\pi /e}$ in $\mathbb R^3$. This follows from [ SunWang2025 ] , Example 3.6 and Corollary 2.4 with Lemma 2.5, PDF pp. 8–11; it is not an identity for the fixed-center Gaussian area of the bowl. title: 3.3 Rotational translating catenoids (Clutterbuck–Schnürer–Schulze, 2005)
text: 72E3A9DEA98C For every neck radius $R>0$ and $n\geq 2$, there is a rotational translating hypersurface with two ends. These are also called winglike translators. They move upward with unit speed. A convenient numerical description uses meridian arclength $s$ and tangent angle $\alpha $: \[  r'=\cos \alpha ,\qquad z'=\sin \alpha ,\qquad \alpha '=\cos \alpha -\frac{n-1}{r}\sin \alpha , \qquad (r,z,\alpha )(0)=(R,0,\pi /2).  \] Revolution gives $(r(s)\omega ,z(s)+t)$ with $\omega \in S^{n-1}$ and $t\in \mathbb R$. The arclength system is obtained from $\vec H=e_{n+1}^{\perp }$ and is not a closed formula. The surface is complete, embedded, noncompact and nonconvex, with topology $S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$. In $\mathbb R^3$ it is an annulus, not an entire graph. Outside the neck the two ends are radial graphs. Each has expansion \[  f_\pm (r)=\frac{r^2}{2(n-1)}-\log r+C_\pm +O(r^{-1}).  \] In particular the two ends go to spatial infinity and the complete surface is proper. The parameter controls the neck radius. The supplied survey describes the limiting double bowl with a singular point on the axis as the neck parameter tends to zero. See [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Section 4, PDF page 10. The original construction and end expansion are [ CSS07 ] , Lemma 2.3, PDF pages 5–7 of the author preprint. title: 3.9 Strictly convex delta-wing translators
text: B72E7DC6B42E For every $b>\pi /2$, there is a complete strictly convex unit-speed translator that is a graph $z=u_ b(x,y)$ over \[  (x,y)\in \mathbb R\times (-b,b),\qquad \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{(u_ b)_ i(u_ b)_ j}{1+|Du_ b|^2}\right)(u_ b)_{ij}=1.  \] This is a nonlinear PDE characterization; no explicit height formula is supplied. The graph is embedded, noncompact, diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^2$, and has positive Gauss curvature everywhere. After centering and a vertical translation, $u_ b(0,0)=0$ is its minimum and $u_ b$ is even in both coordinates. The width is exactly $2b>\pi $. Among complete translators on this strip that are not tilted grim reapers, it is unique up to translation. The centered solution depends smoothly on compact sets under limits of the width parameter. Along the two unbounded horizontal directions, translated graphs converge smoothly to the two oppositely tilted grim-reaper cylinders of the same strip width. Their angle is determined by \[  \cos \theta =\frac{\pi }{2b}.  \] This relation follows from the explicit tilted-cylinder width; the supplied preprint has an inverted ratio in its printed statement of Theorem 2.4. Graphical weighted stability holds. This is a strictly convex surface, whereas the tilted grim-reaper cylinders on the same strip have zero Gauss curvature. See [ HIMWGraphical18 ] , Theorems 1.1, 2.4, 4.1 and 5.7 and Corollary 5.5 (PDF pages 4, 6, 10–12). The construction, uniqueness, and asymptotic results are cited rather than reproduced here. The illustration numerically approximates the rectangular Dirichlet construction in Sections 3–4 at $b=\pi /\sqrt{2}$, then recenters at the minimum and displays a compact height-truncated patch. The paper uses downward translation; the picture reflects the vertical coordinate to match the upward convention here. B72E7DC6B42E For every $b>\pi /2$, there is a complete strictly convex unit-speed translator that is a graph $z=u_ b(x,y)$ over \[  (x,y)\in \mathbb R\times (-b,b),\qquad \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{(u_ b)_ i(u_ b)_ j}{1+|Du_ b|^2}\right)(u_ b)_{ij}=1.  \] This is a nonlinear PDE characterization; no explicit height formula is supplied. After centering and a vertical translation, $u_ b(0,0)=0$ is its minimum and $u_ b$ is even in both coordinates. The width is exactly $2b>\pi $. Among complete translators on this strip that are not tilted grim reapers, it is unique up to translation. The centered solution depends smoothly on compact sets under limits of the width parameter. Along the two unbounded horizontal directions, translated graphs converge smoothly to the two oppositely tilted grim-reaper cylinders of the same strip width. title: 3.16 Nonrotational entire convex translators
text: 0F00F9295CD9 In every dimension $n\geq 3$, Xu-Jia Wang constructs entire convex solutions $u:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$ of the unit-speed upward translator equation \[  \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{u_ i u_ j}{1+|Du|^2}\right)u_{ij}=1  \] whose level sets are not spheres or round cylinders in any orthogonal coordinate system. This is an existence construction, not an explicit formula. The graphs are embedded, complete, proper and diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$; the last three facts also follow directly from being smooth entire graphs. Their flows exist for all $t\in \mathbb R$ by translation. They are convex and break the spherical or cylindrical rotational pattern of the bowl and its Euclidean products. The corresponding statement for complete entire graphs in $\mathbb R^3$ is false: there the bowl is the only example. Under spatial blow-down $u_ h(x)=h^{-1}u(\sqrt h\, x)$, Wang's theorem gives, after rotations depending on $h$, a quadratic limit of the form \[  \frac{x_1^2+\cdots +x_ k^2}{2(k-1)},\qquad 2\leq k\leq n.  \] The theorem does not rule out slow rotation of the axes as $h\to \infty $. No uniqueness theorem for the general higher-dimensional families is claimed here. For the construction in Section 5, write $x'=(x_1,\ldots ,x_{n-1})$. title: 3.10 Translators with prescribed apex curvatures
text: D68656E88625 Let $k_1,\ldots ,k_ n\geq 0$ with $\sum _ i k_ i=1$. Hoffman–Ilmanen–Martín–White construct a complete properly embedded translating graph over an open domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$. After reflecting their downward convention to upward translation, it satisfies \[  \min u=u(0)=0,\qquad D^2u(0)=\operatorname {diag}(k_1,\ldots ,k_ n).  \] These equations specify apex data, not an explicit global formula. The function is even in every coordinate. If $k_ i=0$ it is invariant under translation in the $i$-th coordinate; if $k_ i>0$, then $D_ i u$ has the same sign as $x_ i$ away from $x_ i=0$. Equal apex curvatures $k_ i=k_ j$ give invariance under rotations in the $(x_ i,x_ j)$-plane. The domain is either all of $\mathbb R^ n$ or a slab $\{ |x_ i|<b\} $. In the slab case the corresponding $k_ i$ is strictly larger than every other $k_ j$. If the two largest prescribed curvatures are equal, the resulting graph is entire. The supplied edition obtains an $(n-2)$-parameter family of pairwise noncongruent entire examples this way. The construction gives existence and the listed symmetries, but does not assert general uniqueness or convexity of every higher-dimensional graph. In particular, apex positivity alone is not a global convexity theorem. See [ HIMWGraphical18 ] , Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 8.2, PDF page 18. The source also has a prescribed-width slab construction in Section 11; its final discussion explicitly leaves general convexity open. For $n=2$, the figure compares three surface cases in $\mathbb R^3$: $(k_1,k_2)=(0,1)$ gives the grim-reaper cylinder $u(x,y)=-\log \cos y$ on $\mathbb R\times (-\pi /2,\pi /2)$, while $(1/2,1/2)$ gives the rotational bowl. The intermediate picture reuses a numerical $\Delta $-wing on the strip $\mathbb R\times (-\pi /\sqrt2,\pi /\sqrt2)$, obtained by the rectangular Dirichlet construction in Sections 3–4; its measured apex Hessian is approximately $(0.2443,0.7557)$, not an exact prescribed pair. The bowl profile is integrated numerically. All three translate by $t e_3$ for $t\in \mathbb R$. The principal-section view compares the graph with the local Taylor data $\frac12 k_ i s^2$; those parabolas are not global translator formulas. title: 3.11 Scherkenoid translators (Hoffman–Martín–White, 2019)
text: C6C5A44F27CC Hoffman–Martín–White construct Scherkenoids for $0<\alpha <\pi $ and $w\geq \pi $ as complete, properly embedded, singly periodic translator surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$; see [ HMW20 ] , Theorems 2.3 and 9.2. In the catalogue's upward convention, the fundamental piece is the graph of $U$ over \[  \Omega (\alpha ,w)=\{ (x,y):0<y<w,\  x>y\cot \alpha \} ,  \] with $U\to +\infty $ on the two horizontal rays and $U\to -\infty $ on the finite slanted edge. The graph closes along the two vertical lines above the corners. Repeated half-turns about those lines produce the complete surface, with period $2(w\cot \alpha ,w,0)$. This is a boundary-value construction, not a closed formula for $U$. The connected illustration fixes $\alpha =\pi /2$ and allows $w$ to vary. It shows how a single central sheet opens into alternating wings. Far along a wing, after recentering height, the limiting graph has the explicit profile \[  G_ w(x,y)=-\left(\frac{w}{\pi }\right)^2\log \sin \left(\frac{\pi y}{w}\right) +x\sqrt{\left(\frac{w}{\pi }\right)^2-1},\qquad x\in \mathbb R,\quad 0<y<w.  \] This formula describes the tilted grim-reaper limit, not the whole Scherkenoid. For $w=\pi $ the tilt vanishes. In the upward convention, the height limits are the plane $x=y\cot \alpha $ as $z\to -\infty $ and the planes $y=nw$, $n\in \mathbb Z$, as $z\to +\infty $. The drawing follows Figures 5 and 11 and Section 9 of [ HMW20 ] , arXiv version 4, pages 7 and 26–30. Its joining profile is schematic, not a numerical solution of the translator equation. The paper uses downward velocity; reflecting height gives the upward flow $M_ t=M+t e_3$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. See also the earlier survey [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Section 5. No stability or entropy conclusion is inferred from the drawing. title: 3.12 The pitchfork translator (Hoffman–Martín–White, 2019)
text: B5E7AB44607B The pitchfork is a complete, properly embedded, simply connected, nongraphical translator in $\mathbb R^3$. The supplied notes describe it as a limit of Scherk-type examples, without an explicit formula. It has genus zero. This distinguishes it from Nguyen's periodic infinite-genus tridents despite their similar asymptotic plane arrangements. After reflection to upward translation, it is asymptotic to one plane as $z\to -\infty $ and to three parallel planes as $z\to +\infty $. These are height-direction asymptotics, not a claim that the surface has four topological ends. Its translation yields an eternal noncompact flow. The later construction paper records finite topology and quadratic area growth for its pitchfork subfamily. See [ HIMWNotes19 ] , Section 5 and Figure 7, PDF pages 11–12, and [ HMW20 ] . The existence proof is external. The full construction supplies a pitchfork for each half-width $w\geq \pi $, lying in $|y|<w$. Theorem 1 of [ MSTW26 ] proves uniqueness up to isometry for fixed width in this semigraphical family. Moreover, [ GMM25 ] , Theorem 1.5, characterizes pitchforks among complete embedded simply connected translators of finite width, entropy $3$, and containing a vertical line. These hypotheses are essential to the stated classification. To read the picture, remove the vertical $z$-axis. One component is a graph $z=v(x,y)$ over $\mathbb R\times (0,w)$; the other is its image under $(x,y,z)\mapsto (-x,-y,z)$. In the upward convention the boundary values are \[  v(x,0)=-\infty \quad (x<0),\qquad v(x,0)=+\infty \quad (x>0),\qquad v(x,w)=+\infty .  \] Theorem 12.1 and Corollary 12.2 of [ HMW20 ] give the smooth extension along the axis, negative Gauss curvature, and the planar and tilted-grim-reaper asymptotics. For $w=\pi $, the grim-reaper profile, after vertical recentering at $y=\pi /2$, is $-\log \sin y$ for $0<y<\pi $. This is an asymptotic profile, not a formula for the pitchfork. The interactive drawing illustrates this width using two colored halves and horizontal sections, following Figures 6 and 14 of that paper. Its connecting geometry is schematic, not a computed solution of the translator equation. text: 27C982677562 Nguyen's tridents are complete periodic embedded translating surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ obtained by desingularizing a grim-reaper cylinder and a plane. We use unit upward velocity $e_3$, so $M_ t=M_0+t e_3$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. There is no explicit global formula for the completed translator. They are noncompact and have infinite genus. A repeating row of Scherk saddle connections resolves the intersection; the intersecting input surfaces are not themselves a trident. In the upward convention there is one asymptotic plane as $z\to -\infty $ and three parallel asymptotic planes as $z\to +\infty $. These describe height-direction asymptotics, not a count of topological ends of the full periodic surface. Nguyen's construction applies at sufficiently small positive scales. The later semigraphical construction agrees with these examples in that range; its tridents are properly embedded and have entropy $3$ [ HMWTridents22 ] , Theorem 1 and pp. 2–3. This entropy is not identified with centered Gaussian area. The local minimal ingredient is $\sin v=\sinh u\sinh w$, with $(u,v,w)\in \mathbb R^3$ and period $2\pi $ in $v$. Its four wings are attached to two planar wings and two grim-reaper wings. In the unit upward convention the limiting inputs are $z=-\log \cos y$, $|y|<\pi /2$, $x\in \mathbb R$, and the plane $y=0$. See [ Nguyen09 ] , Theorem 1, Sections 1.2–1.4 and Section 2 (Definitions 4–5), and [ HMWTridents22 ] , Figures 1–2. The latter figures use downward translation; here height is reflected. In particular, its fixed illustrative half-width $\pi /2$ is the limiting input width, not the width of a finite-period trident. text: 85D3C19BE7E6 Dávila–del Pino–Nguyen construct complete embedded orientable translating surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ with finite topology and large genus. The construction desingularizes an intersecting bowl translator and translating catenoid. It is a gluing construction, not an explicit formula. The examples have three asymptotically paraboloidal ends. They are noncompact; their translation gives an eternal flow. u _ A(x)],zight): x\in S_ A,\  z\geq z_0ight\} ,\qquad \| u(\cdot ,z)\| _{C^0(S_ A)}=O(z^{-\epsilon })  \] for some $\epsilon >0$. The unknown function $u$ is solved for by the construction. In particular, the auxiliary expression obtained by setting $u=0$ is not asserted to be a translator. The translators have codimension one and are smooth, noncompact, complete, and properly embedded. section: 3.22 Translators with high-genus spherical-doubling ends (Sun–Zhihan Wang, 2023)
text: 9B1B88A4317F Fix an integer $m$ sufficiently large. In the spherical-doubling construction of Kapouleas–McGrath, choose two latitude circles and $m$ aligned bridge sites on each circle. Their theorem gives a smooth closed embedded shrinker $S_ m\subset \mathbb R^3$, obtained by connecting two nearby copies of the radius-two sphere with $2m$ small catenoidal bridges. Its genus is $2m-1$. This specifies a concrete subfamily of their construction; there is no effective lower threshold for $m$ or explicit formula for $S_ m$ in this statement. Applying the Sun–Wang construction to $S_ m$ produces complete embedded translators $\Sigma _ m^3\subset \mathbb R^4$ with \[  \vec H_{\Sigma _ m}=e_4^\perp ,\qquad M_ t=\Sigma _ m+t e_4,\quad t\in \mathbb R,  \] and, outside a compact set, \[  \Sigma _ m= \left\{ \left(\sqrt z\, [x+u_ m(x,z)\nu _{S_ m}(x)],z\right): x\in S_ m,\  z\geq z_0\right\} ,\qquad \| u_ m(\cdot ,z)\| _{C^0(S_ m)}=O(z^{-\epsilon _ m})  \] for some $\epsilon _ m>0$. Both the shrinker and the translator are existence constructions; the displayed formula contains an unknown correction and is not an explicit solution. Each translator is a smooth, complete, properly embedded, noncompact hypersurface, with one end diffeomorphic to $S_ m\times [z_0,\infty )$. The genus $2m-1$ belongs to the two-dimensional horizontal cross-section. No surface genus or complete three-manifold topology is assigned to $\Sigma _ m$. The unique tangent flow at backward infinity is generated by $S_ m\times \mathbb R$ with multiplicity one. Thus these examples have a different prescribed shrinker from the Angenent-torus-end examples, the bowl, and the previously catalogued three-ended translating surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$. For each fixed $S_ m$ the end construction has $I_ m=\operatorname {ind}_ F(S_ m)$ parameters before quotienting by ambient translations. The exact index is not computed by the cited construction. One may choose an end and a minimizing completion invariant under the finite symmetry group $\mathcal G_ m=D_{2m}\times \mathbb Z_2$ of order $4m$, where $D_{2m}$ here denotes the dihedral group of order $2m$. Symmetry is asserted for such selected examples, not for every member of the full $I_ m$-parameter family. The completions are locally $\mathcal I$-minimizing for $\mathcal I=\int e^ z\, d\mathcal H^3$, hence stable for compactly supported variations of that functional. The generic uniqueness result concerns minimizing completions exponentially asymptotic to a fixed constructed end. No specific fattening example for these $S_ m$ is proved in the cited sources. The entropy is exactly the Gaussian area of the prescribed shrinker: \[  \lambda (\Sigma _ m)=F(S_ m)=\lambda (S_ m)<2F(S^2(2))=\frac8e.  \] The strict upper bound follows by applying the area inequality of Kapouleas–McGrath in the Gaussian metric $g=e^{-|x|^2/4}g_{\rm Euc}$ and dividing its surface area by $4\pi $. It is a consequence of the two cited theorems, not a numerical approximation. No individual numerical entropy or value of $F_{0,1}(\Sigma _ m)$ is recorded. For the input shrinkers, see [ KapouleasMcGrath2023 ] , Theorem 10.5, with $k_\circ =2$ and $\mathbf m=(m)$ (arXiv version 4, PDF page 66), Theorem 9.40 (page 65), and Definitions 7.10–7.11 and Remark 7.12 (page 40). The genus is $|L|-1=2m-1$; smooth embeddedness and the Gaussian-metric area inequality follow from Theorem 5.7 and equation (5.9) (page 30; also Theorem A on page 3). The application to translators uses [ SunWang2025 ] , Theorems 3.7 and 4.1 (pages 12 and 28), with compact core and entropy as in Lemma 2.5 and Corollary 2.4 (pages 8–10). title: 3.13 Doubly periodic Scherk translators (Hoffman–Martín–White, 2019)
text: D24DEEE97A5F For every $0<\alpha <\pi $ and $0<w<\pi $, Hoffman–Martín–White construct a complete properly embedded translator in $\mathbb R^3$. In their downward convention, a fundamental piece is a graph over the parallelogram of height $w$, angle $\alpha $, and a uniquely selected base length $L(\alpha ,w)>0$, with boundary values $-\infty $ on the horizontal sides and $+\infty $ on the other sides. Half-turns about its four vertical boundary lines extend it to the complete doubly periodic surface. Reflecting $z$ gives our upward normalization $\mathbf H=e_3^\perp $ and the eternal flow $M_ t=M+te_3$, $t\in \mathbb R$. This is an elliptic boundary-value construction, not Scherk's explicit minimal-surface formula. The surface has infinite genus and strictly negative Gauss curvature. Its infinitely many asymptotic parallel planes force infinite entropy. The topological end count and centered Gaussian area are not evaluated here. Uniqueness up to ambient isometry holds for the specified angle and width. Stability of a graphical fundamental piece does not establish stability of the full reflected surface. The illustration uses the rectangular case $\alpha =w=\pi /2$ in Figures 3 and 8 of the source. In the upward convention, the centred fundamental graph $z=v(x,y)$ satisfies \[  \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{v_ i v_ j}{1+|Dv|^2}\right)v_{ij}=1, \qquad (x,y)\in (-L/2,L/2)\times (-w/2,w/2),  \] with $v\to +\infty $ on $y=\pm w/2$ and $v\to -\infty $ on $x=\pm L/2$. The base length is selected by the boundary-value problem, not an independent parameter; Theorem 5.1 gives $L>w$ in this rectangular case. The picture follows the finite-boundary construction in the proof of Theorem 3.1: replace the infinite data by $\pm 2.5$, impose $v(0,0)=0$, and solve numerically for both $v$ and $L$. A $257\times 257$ grid gives $L\approx 2.4483$ for this truncated problem. This number is not a certified value of the infinite-boundary length. Only $|z|\le 1.5$ is displayed. The small unresolved regions at the four vertical corner lines are filled by interpolation; the remaining surface comes from the numerical graph. The periodic view repeats the patch by vertical half-turns, preserving height, and shows finitely many copies of the resulting infinite arrangement. In centred coordinates these graph domains occupy alternating rectangles, with horizontal periods $(2L,0,0)$ and $(0,2w,0)$. The height slider changes only the displayed truncation. Neither mesh refinement nor the small discrete residual supplies a certified error bound for the complete translator. Sources: [ HMW20 ] , Theorems 2.3, 3.1, 5.1 and 6.1, Figures 3 and 8–10, and the discussion on pp. 9 and 17; [ MSTW26 ] , Theorem 1. title: 3.14 Helicoid-like translators (Hoffman–Martín–White, 2019)
text: E6CC94303132 For each $0<w<\pi $, there is a complete properly embedded helicoid-like translator in $\mathbb R^3$. In the downward convention, its fundamental graph over $\mathbb R\times (0,w)$ has alternating infinite boundary values, switching at $(0,0)$ and $(\widehat x,w)$, where $\widehat x>0$ is selected by the solution. Half-turn reflection about the two vertical boundary lines gives horizontal period $2(\widehat x,w,0)$. Reflection in a horizontal plane converts it to $M_ t=M+te_3$, $t\in \mathbb R$. It is noncompact and has strictly negative Gauss curvature. Successive simply connected strip pieces join along a line in a chain, giving a plane topologically, with genus zero and one topological end. This is a topological deduction from the strip decomposition. Its asymptotic family of parallel vertical planes implies $\lambda (M)=+\infty $. No centered Gaussian-area value is recorded. The axis is oblique to these planes; an ordinary minimal helicoid is not this translator. Sources: [ HMW20 ] , Theorems 2.3 and 11.1 and Remark 11.2; [ MSTW26 ] , Theorem 1 and Section 4, proves uniqueness up to isometry for fixed fundamental width. The earlier paper's open uniqueness question is therefore superseded. The picture shows only the semigraphical arrangement, not a numerical PDE solution. title: 3.15 Annuloid translators in slabs (Hoffman–Martín–White, 2023)
text: 4887FC9B88DC For every inner half-width $b\geq \pi /2$ and necksize $s>0$, Hoffman–Martín–White construct a complete properly embedded annular translator in $\mathbb R^3$. Their necksize is the distance from the $z$-axis to $M\cap \{ y=0\} $; it is not assumed to be a circular neck radius. The surface lies in a slab $|y|\leq B$, has both vertical coordinate-plane reflection symmetries, and is nonrotational. Its topology is $S^1\times \mathbb R$: genus zero and two ends. After reflecting the source's downward translator, $M_ t=M+te_3$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. The positive-height asymptotics are four planes $y=\pm b,\pm B$, counted with multiplicity if $b=B$; the negative-height end of the ambient space sees no surface. Four asymptotic planes in one height direction do not mean four topological ends. The outer half-width $B$ is an output of the construction, not an independent prescribed parameter. Capped and uncapped behaviors occur. No closed formula or uniqueness for fixed $(b,s)$ is supplied. The entropy is exactly $4$, by [ HMWAnnuli24 ] , Remark 7.9, using [ GMM25 ] , Corollary 8.5. title: 3.17 Joyce–Lee–Tsui small-angle Lagrangian translators
text: The following unit-speed translators have dimension and codimension $n$ in $\mathbb C^ n$. BCD2A9973070 (Almost-calibrated translating Lagrangians) Fix $n\geq 2$ and $a_1,\ldots ,a_{n-1}>0$. Define the positive smooth function \[  P(y)=\frac{e^{y^2}\prod _{j=1}^{n-1}(1+a_ jy^2)-1}{y^2}, \qquad P(0)=1+\sum _{j=1}^{n-1}a_ j,  \] and the quadratures \[  \phi _ j(y)=\int _0^ y\frac{dt}{(a_ j^{-1}+t^2)\sqrt{P(t)}},\qquad B(y)=\int _0^ y\frac{dt}{\sqrt{P(t)}}.  \] For $(x,y)\in \mathbb R^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$, set \[  X(x,y)=\left(x_ j\sqrt{a_ j^{-1}+y^2}\, e^{i\phi _ j(y)}\right)_{j=1}^{n-1} \mathbin {\times }\left(\tfrac 12(y^2-|x|^2)+iB(y)\right).  \] Here the displayed product concatenates complex coordinates. This is Corollary I of [ JoyceLeeTsui2010 ] with $\alpha =1$, after a constant imaginary translation in the last coordinate. Differentiating the source's angle expression gives $\theta '=-1/\sqrt P$, so this integral form avoids a choice of argument branch. The image is a complete proper embedded Lagrangian $\mathbb R^ n$ with one topological end. It satisfies $\vec H=V^\perp $ for $V=(0,\ldots ,0,1)$ and evolves as $X+tV$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. If $\bar\phi _ j=\lim _{y\to \infty }\phi _ j(y)$, then $0<\sum _ j\bar\phi _ j<\pi /2$ and the angle oscillation is $\pi -2\sum _ j\bar\phi _ j$; it can be arbitrarily small. The plane-pair description in the source is heuristic, not an asserted smooth asymptotic-cone theorem. The figure uses numerical quadrature of this exact integral parametrization in $\mathbb C^2$, followed by projection. The image is a complete proper embedded Lagrangian $\mathbb R^ n$ with one topological end. It satisfies $\vec H=V^\perp $ for $V=(0,\ldots ,0,1)$ and evolves as $X+tV$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. If $\bar\phi _ j=\lim _{y\to \infty }\phi _ j(y)$, then $0<\sum _ j\bar\phi _ j<\pi /2$ and the angle oscillation is $\pi -2\sum _ j\bar\phi _ j$; it can be arbitrarily small. The plane-pair description in the source is heuristic, not an asserted smooth asymptotic-cone theorem. The figure uses numerical quadrature of this exact integral parametrization in $\mathbb C^2$, followed by projection.

title: 3.18 Explicit rotating Lagrangian translators
text: An elementary subfamily of the same quadric ansatz has unbounded Lagrangian angle. A19CAED49B0D (Rotating translating planes) For $n\geq 2$, put $k=n-1$. The exact map \[  X(x,s)=\left(x_1e^{is},\ldots ,x_ ke^{is},\tfrac 12|x|^2-is\right), \qquad (x,s)\in \mathbb R^ k\times \mathbb R,  \] is a complete proper embedded Lagrangian in $\mathbb C^ n$, of dimension and codimension $n$. Its translator velocity is $V=(0,\ldots ,0,k)$, so $X+tV$, $t\in \mathbb R$, is eternal. Spatial dilation by $k$ gives unit translating speed if desired. This is the constant-radius case of Theorem G and Corollary H of [ JoyceLeeTsui2010 ] , with $\lambda _ j=-1$, $a_ j=A=1$, $u=0$, and $\alpha =k$. Directly, the metric and a lifted angle are \[  g=\sum _ jdx_ j^2+\left(\sum _ jx_ jdx_ j\right)^2+(1+|x|^2)ds^2, \qquad \theta =ks-\pi /2.  \] Consequently \[  \vec H=J\nabla \theta =\frac{k}{1+|x|^2}(-x_1e^{is},\ldots ,-x_ ke^{is},1)=V^\perp .  \] The last imaginary coordinate recovers $s$, proving injectivity; $|X|^2=|x|^2+|x|^4/4+s^2$ proves properness. The metric dominates the Euclidean domain metric, proving completeness. Topologically it is $\mathbb R^ n$, with one end. It has a combined rotation and imaginary-translation symmetry and is not almost calibrated. No stability or entropy value is claimed. title: 3.24 Su translators obtained by gluing grim cylinders

section: 3.24 Su translators obtained by gluing grim cylinders
text: 164F129D254D (Lawlor-neck desingularizations of grim cylinders) Fix $m\geq 3$. Let \[  \gamma _0(u)=-\log \cos u-i(u-\pi /2),\quad |u|<\pi /2,\qquad L_0=\mathbb R^{m-1}\times \gamma _0((-\pi /2,\pi /2))\subset \mathbb C^ m.  \] Choose $\phi _ j\in (0,\pi )$ with $\sum _{j=1}^ m\phi _ j=\pi $, and $\lambda \in \mathbb R$. Define \[  P_{\phi ,\lambda }(z)=(e^{i\phi _1}z_1,\ldots ,e^{i\phi _{m-1}}z_{m-1},z_ m+\lambda +i\phi _ m).  \] The two grim cylinders meet at one transverse point and satisfy the tangent-plane angle criterion. Su proves that for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$ their intersection can be replaced by a Lawlor neck and then perturbed to a smooth embedded Lagrangian translator $L_\varepsilon $, diffeomorphic to $S^{m-1}\times \mathbb R$. It is complete and proper, with two ends approaching the original cylinder ends in the weighted construction. Its dimension and codimension are $m$. With $e_ m$ the real unit vector in the last complex coordinate, \[  \vec H=e_ m^\perp ,\qquad L_{\varepsilon ,t}=L_\varepsilon +t e_ m,\qquad -\infty <t<\infty .  \] The parameter $\varepsilon $ is a gluing scale, not flow time. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ the translators converge as currents to $L_0\cup P_{\phi ,\lambda }(L_0)$. The displayed formula is for the building blocks; the perturbed translator has no closed formula. Properness and completeness follow from the small decaying graph on the complete proper ends and the compact neck region. Source: [ Su2022 ] , Main Theorem (p. 3), Sections 3.2–3.4 (pp. 8–10), Section 4.1 (pp. 11–12), and Theorem 6.10 (p. 28). Its Corollary 1.1 also gives examples with arbitrarily many ends and noncontractible loops by finite admissible arrangements of grim cylinders. Those more general topologies are not assigned to this two-ended case. The construction requires the source's $T$-finite condition; it does not establish gluing arbitrary planes to grim cylinders. No uniqueness, entropy value, or dynamical stability is claimed. The pictures specialize to $m=3$, $\phi _1=\phi _2=\phi _3=\pi /3$, and $\lambda =0$. The common point is \[  p=(0,0,q),\qquad q=-\log \cos (\pi /6)+2\pi i/3.  \] An equal-angle Lawlor neck centered at $p$ can be written, up to its scale, as \[  p+\bigl (w_\varepsilon (s)\omega _1,w_\varepsilon (s)\omega _2, e^{-2\pi i/3}w_\varepsilon (s)\omega _3\bigr ),\qquad w_\varepsilon (s)=\varepsilon (s+i)^{1/3},\quad s\in \mathbb R,\quad \omega \in S^2,  \] where $0<\arg w_\varepsilon <\pi /3$. The identity $\operatorname {Im}(w_\varepsilon ^3)=\varepsilon ^3$ gives the symmetric special Lagrangian neck; it is a local minimal ingredient, not itself the translator. The drawing uses the slice $\omega _2=0$ and an illustrative interpolation to the exact grim cylinders. This coordinate interpolation does not implement Su's potential gluing or final correction. The projected slice retains $(\operatorname {Re}(e^{-i\beta }z_1),\operatorname {Im}z_3,\operatorname {Re}z_3)$; omitted coordinates can create apparent crossings. The profile view selects $\omega _1=\omega _2=0$, and does not determine the topology of the full translator. section: 4.3 Expanding smoothings of planar corners (Halldórsson, 2010; Ding, 2015)
text: The convention throughout these entries is $\vec H=X^\perp /2$ for the time-one profile. Thus $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M$, $t>0$, is the corresponding flow. The positive weight for variational statements is $e^{|X|^2/4}$; minimizing this weighted area locally will be called $E$-minimizing. 72808FA576A9 (Even graphical corner expanders) For every $\kappa >0$ there is a smooth even function $\phi _\kappa :\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$ satisfying \[  \frac{\phi _\kappa ''}{1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2} +\frac{x\phi _\kappa '-\phi _\kappa }{2}=0, \qquad \phi _\kappa '(0)=0, \qquad \lim _{|x|\to \infty }\frac{\phi _\kappa (x)}{|x|}=\kappa .  \] The profile $\Gamma _\kappa =\{ (x,\phi _\kappa (x)):x\in \mathbb R\} $ is a smooth complete properly embedded noncompact curve in $\mathbb R^2$, with topology $\mathbb R$, reflection symmetry, and two ends asymptotic to the rays of $y=\kappa |x|$. It is $E$-minimizing against compact replacements. Its curvature vector is nonzero and points along the upward graph normal: writing $q=\phi _\kappa -x\phi _\kappa '$ gives $q'=-x(1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2)q/2$ and $\phi _\kappa ''=(1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2)q/2$, with $q(0)>0$. The source gives the quantitative estimate, for $x>0$, \[  0\leq \phi _\kappa (x)-\kappa x \leq \min \left\{ \frac{2e(\kappa +2)}{x}e^{-x^2/4},\, 3\kappa +2\right\} .  \] The flow $\sqrt t\, \Gamma _\kappa $, $t\in (0,\infty )$, smooths the corner at time zero. These are ODE-defined profiles, not elementary closed formulas. Source: [ Ding20 ] , Section 4, equations (4.9)–(4.15), printed pp. 373–374, supplied PDF pp. 15–16. The figure shows a numerical ODE profile with $\phi (0)=1$. Taking the product with $\mathbb R$ gives an example in $\mathbb R^3$ with one zero principal curvature. For the planar classification, including the stationary-line endpoint, see [ Halldorsson2012 ] , Theorem 6.1, PDF pp. 13–15. section: 4.7 Rotational graphical expanders over round cones
text: D3CC5E948716 (Entire radial cone smoothings) For $n\geq 2$ and $\kappa >0$, consider \[  M_\kappa =\{ (x,\phi _\kappa (|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\} \subset \mathbb R^{n+1},  \] where $\phi _\kappa $ is the smooth radial solution constructed with \[  \frac{\phi _\kappa ''}{1+(\phi _\kappa ')^2} +\frac{n-1}{r}\phi _\kappa ' +\frac{r\phi _\kappa '-\phi _\kappa }{2}=0, \qquad \phi _\kappa '(0)=0, \qquad \lim _{r\to \infty }\frac{\phi _\kappa (r)}r=\kappa .  \] The equation at $r=0$ is interpreted by smooth radial extension; it implies $\phi _\kappa ''(0)=\phi _\kappa (0)/(2n)$. This is an ODE construction, not a closed formula. The hypersurface is smooth, complete, properly embedded, noncompact, rotationally symmetric, diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$, and $E$-minimizing against compact replacements. It has one conical end and nondecreasing height. The estimate \[  0\leq \phi _\kappa (r)-\kappa r \leq ((n+1)\kappa +2)\min \{ 1,r^{-1}\} ,\qquad r>0,  \] records the rate at which it approaches its cone. Its flow is $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M_\kappa $ for $t>0$, with initial cone $z=\kappa |x|$. Source: [ Ding20 ] , Section 4, equations (4.1), (4.7), and (4.8), printed pp. 371–373, supplied PDF pp. 13–15. title: 4.5 Two-sheeted expanders of rotational double cones

section: 4.5 Two-sheeted expanders of rotational double cones
text: 4F35D93CA4BD (Disconnected double-cone smoothings) Let $n\geq 2$, write $(x,z)\in \mathbb R^ n\times \mathbb R$, and let \[  D_\alpha =\{ (x,z):|x|=|z|\tan \alpha \} ,\qquad 0<\alpha <\pi /2.  \] With $\phi _{\cot \alpha }$ from Example 4.7 , the two-sheeted expander is \[  M_\alpha ^{(2)} =\{ (x,\phi _{\cot \alpha }(|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\}  \mathbin {\cup } \{ (x,-\phi _{\cot \alpha }(|x|)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\} .  \] This display specifies the surface using ODE-defined functions. Its two components are smooth, complete, properly embedded convex entire graphs, each diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. The union is noncompact, invariant under rotations about the $z$-axis and under $z\mapsto -z$, and has two oppositely directed conical ends. The flow $\sqrt t\, M_\alpha ^{(2)}$, $t>0$, approaches $D_\alpha $ as $t\downarrow 0$. Existence and uniqueness of each rotational single-lobe graphical profile are established in [ AIC95 ] , Lemma 2(i), printed p. 1947, supplied PDF p. 12. Theorem 4, printed pp. 1950–1951, PDF pp. 15–16, provides a critical angle $\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)\in (0,\pi /2)$. For $\alpha <\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)$ the level-set flow of the double cone is exactly the two-sheeted flow. For angles above this threshold there are also connected smoothings, so the graphical uniqueness statement does not assert uniqueness among all flows from the cone. The critical-angle decimal estimates later in that paper are numerical. section: 4.6 One-sheeted expanders of rotational double cones
text: 3A4775A9BD2C (Connected double-cone smoothings) For $n\geq 2$ and a neck parameter $a>0$, the initial value problem \[  u''=(1+(u')^2)\left(\frac{n-1}{u}+\frac{u-zu'}2\right), \qquad u(0)=a,\quad u'(0)=0,  \] defines a positive, smooth, even profile on $\mathbb R$. Rotating it gives \[  M_ a=\{ (u(z)\omega ,z):z\in \mathbb R,\  \omega \in S^{n-1}\}  \subset \mathbb R^{n+1}.  \] This is a smooth complete properly embedded noncompact expander with topology $S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$, rotational symmetry, reflection symmetry, and two conical ends. The profile is increasing for $z>0$. Its limiting aperture depends on $a$; the formula is an ODE specification, not an elementary expression. The evolution is $\sqrt t\, M_ a$ for $t>0$. For every $\alpha >\alpha _{\rm crit}(n+1)$ there exists such a connected expander asymptotic to $D_\alpha $ from Example 4.5 . It gives a second thin evolution from that cone alongside the disconnected two-sheeted solution. The cited theorem uses a strict inequality and does not establish a universal uniqueness assertion for the one-sheeted profile. Source: [ AIC95 ] , Lemma 2(ii), Lemma 3, and Theorem 4, printed pp. 1947–1951, supplied PDF pp. 12–16. title: 4.8 One-sided expanders from mean-convex cones
text: A6044506F79A (Ding's smooth minimizing expanders) Let $C\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be an $n$-dimensional $C^{3,\beta }$-regular cone, $0<\beta <1$, regular away from its vertex, with a $C^{3,\beta }$ embedded link in $S^ n$. Assume that $C$ is mean convex but not area minimizing, that $\partial \Omega =C$, and that its mean curvature vector points into the chosen domain $\Omega $ wherever it is nonzero. Then there is a unique smooth complete embedded $E$-minimizing self-expanding hypersurface $M\subset \Omega $ with tangent cone $C$ at infinity. Its mean curvature vector is everywhere nonzero and points into $\Omega $, and \[  \{ \sqrt t\, M:t>0\}   \] is a foliation of $\Omega $ moving by mean curvature flow. The normalization is $\vec H=X^\perp /2$. This is an existence theorem for a family determined by the cone and the chosen side, not an explicit parametrization. The uniqueness just stated includes the chosen-side and minimizing hypotheses. Its topology, symmetry, and number of ends depend on the chosen cone. Source: [ Ding20 ] , Theorem 1.1, printed p. 361, supplied PDF p. 3, and Theorem 6.12, printed pp. 402–403, PDF pp. 44–45. The broader minimizing-current existence theorem in that paper can have singularities and is not being substituted for this smooth theorem. The figure is a schematic of the cone, selected domain, and expanding leaves. title: 4.2 Self-expanding planar tree networks (Mazzeo–Saez, 2007)
text: 16898F334139 (Regular expanding trees with prescribed rays) A regular planar network consists of smooth branches meeting only at triple junctions, with angles $120$ degrees at every junction. A self-expanding network $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^2$ satisfies \[  \vec k=\frac{X^\perp }{2}  \] on each open branch; its time evolution is $\Sigma _ t=\sqrt t\, \Sigma $, $t>0$, with the same angle condition. It is a network flow and is not a smooth immersed curve at its junctions. title: 4.9 Mountain-pass self-expanders
text: 1EA720390291 Let $2\leq n\leq 6$, let $C\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a $C^3$-regular cone, and suppose two distinct strictly stable $C^2$-asymptotically conical self-expanders $\Gamma _-\preceq \Gamma _+$ approach $C$. The order means inclusion of their consistently oriented enclosed regions. Bernstein–Wang construct a further smooth properly embedded self-expander $\Gamma _0$ between them, meeting the open intervening region. The associated flow is $M_ t=\sqrt t\, \Gamma _0$, $t>0$, with $\mathbf H=X^\perp /2$. If the cone is generic in the precise sense that every expander asymptotic to it has no nontrivial Jacobi field fixing infinity, $\Gamma _0$ can be chosen unstable for expander weighted area. The theorem does not prescribe its genus, connectedness, symmetry or uniqueness. Completeness follows from proper embeddedness without boundary. Cone asymptotics give Euclidean area growth and hence finite Gaussian area and entropy; no numerical value is supplied. Corollary 1.3 gives an open set of cones admitting at least two connected and one disconnected smoothing, beyond the rotational setting. Sources: [ BWMP20 ] , Theorem 1.1 and Corollaries 1.2–1.3, pp. 1–2. In higher dimensions the general theorem allows a singular set of codimension seven; only its smooth $2\leq n\leq 6$ cases are catalogued here. section: 4.10 Three-ended expanders of positive genus (Shao–Zou, 2025; Hoffman–Martín–White, 2026)
text: 3A8C3B21B572 Hoffman–Martín–White construct connected embedded self-expanders in $\mathbb R^3$ of arbitrarily large genus at a single suitable cone. Precisely, let $C=C_ k$ satisfy the symmetry and three-component link hypotheses of their Theorem 1.1, with its spherical link sufficiently close to the equatorial plane as required in Theorem 1.2. For each odd prime $p$ and integer $a\geq 0$, there are at least four noncongruent $G_ k$-invariant expanders asymptotic to $C$, of genus $p^ a k-1$. These are complete proper noncompact surfaces with three conical ends; the end count follows from the three components of the link. They solve $\mathbf H=X^\perp /2$ and yield $\sqrt t\, E$ for $t>0$. They are obtained by degree theory and limiting constructions, not an explicit formula. No common convexity, stability, or numerical entropy value is asserted. Smooth conical ends imply finite Gaussian area and entropy. The incoming shrinker $M_ k$ has genus $2k-2$. Joining $\sqrt{-t}\, M_ k$ for $t<0$, $C$ at $t=0$, and $\sqrt t\, E$ for $t>0$ gives the source's self-similar Brakke flow, smooth except at the spacetime origin. This is not a genus increase in a smooth flow across $t=0$. Source: [ HMWExpand26 ] , Theorems 1.1–1.2 and equation (1.5), pp. 2–3. The figure is an original topology model, not a numerical solution of the expander equation. The three ends wrap around the $z$-axis, rather than forming three separate tubes. Its displayed cone and small symmetry counts are illustrative; they are not asserted to be the cone $C_ k$ of a constructed shrinker or to satisfy the theorem's quantitative hypotheses. The two slice pairings follow Definition 3.1 and Figure 1 (pp. 9–10): in the reflection plane $\{ y=0\} $, the middle end on the positive-$x$ side is joined to the upper end for type 1, and to the lower end for type 2, with no closed slice curves. Each type has both a small and a big expander. These terms refer to the local integral $\int _ E\phi \, d\mathcal H^2$, below or above the threshold $3/2$, where $\phi $ is a fixed nonnegative radial function supported in $B(0,1/2)$ and normalized by $\int _{\{ z=0\} }\phi \, d\mathcal H^2=1$ (Definition 4.1 and Theorem 4.3). They do not refer to the magnification of the picture. Theorem 5.1 (p. 12) gives all four classes, and Theorems 12.6–12.7 (pp. 39–40) retain genus and class when the boundary radius tends to infinity. Shao–Zou's construction supplies another source of positive-genus three-ended expanders under the dihedral symmetry and sufficiently small cone-angle hypotheses of their main theorem. It uses a desingularization construction and is not a proof that its surfaces are disjoint, as geometric examples, from the other three-ended families cited here. The three ends and surface genus refer to surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$; the homothetic flow is $\sqrt t\, \Sigma $ for $t>0$. title: 4.12 Knotted self-expanders
text: DA3FCE2F354F Mramor–Shengwen Wang construct complete properly embedded self-expanders in $\mathbb R^3$ with knotted topology. Their Theorem 3.1 starts with an embedded orientable surface bounding a handlebody and, with sufficiently many ends, produces an expander whose bounded-region topology realizes that handlebody. These surfaces are stable for the weighted functional $\int e^{|X|^2/4}\, d\mu $; this is expander weighted stability, not entropy stability. A concrete case has genus one and three ends: inside large balls it is isotopic to the boundary of a tubular neighborhood of a trefoil knot with three disks removed and annular ends attached. The half-cylinders in this description specify topology; the constructed geometric ends are asymptotically conical. More generally, every genus $g\geq 1$ occurs with sufficiently many ends, without a universal end count specified here. The normalization is $\mathbf H=X^\perp /2$, with flow $M_ t=\sqrt t\, M$ for $t>0$. The examples are noncompact, complete and proper. No explicit formula, uniqueness, or exact Gaussian-area or entropy value is provided; conical area growth gives finiteness. Source: [ MWKnotted26 ] , Theorems 1.1 and 3.1 and Corollary 3.2, pp. 2 and 8–10, arXiv v1 (November 2, 2026). This is a preprint construction, not independently verified here. The interactive picture shows a trefoil tube with three annular ends, with auxiliary views of the closed tube and its three punctures. The accompanying plate explains these topological operations; Figure 2 of the paper motivates the bridge description. All displayed shapes are schematics, not computed expanders. title: 4.13 Lagrangian expander necks between transverse planes (Joyce–Lee–Tsui, 2008)

section: 4.13 Lagrangian expander necks between transverse planes (Joyce–Lee–Tsui, 2008)
text: These expanders smooth two transverse Lagrangian planes in $\mathbb C^ n$. E25A2DDDEA95 (Expanding Lagrangian necks) Fix $n\geq 2$, $a_ j>0$, and $\psi _ j\in \mathbb R$. Set \[  P_\alpha (y)=\frac{e^{\alpha y^2}\prod _{j=1}^ n(1+a_ jy^2)-1}{y^2}, \quad P_\alpha (0)=\alpha +\sum _ ja_ j,\quad \phi _ j(y)=\psi _ j+\int _0^ y\frac{dt}{(a_ j^{-1}+t^2)\sqrt{P_\alpha (t)}}.  \] With $\alpha =1/2$, the exact integral parametrization \[  X(x,y)=\left(x_ j\sqrt{a_ j^{-1}+y^2}\, e^{i\phi _ j(y)}\right)_{j=1}^ n, \qquad (x,y)\in \mathbb S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R,  \] satisfies $\vec H=X^\perp /2$ and gives the flow $\sqrt t\, X$, $t>0$. By [ JoyceLeeTsui2010 ] , Theorems C–D, its image is a proper embedded Lagrangian neck. It is complete, has dimension and codimension $n$, and has two ends. For $n=2$ its topology is an annulus; generally it is $\mathbb S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$. Write $\bar\phi _ j=\phi _ j(+\infty )-\psi _ j$. The limiting planes have coordinate phases $\psi _ j\pm \bar\phi _ j$, with $0<2\sum _ j\bar\phi _ j<\pi $. Every admissible angle tuple determines unique positive $a_ j$ at fixed $\alpha $ within this family. The neck is zero-Maslov and almost calibrated. Equal $a_ j$ and equal $\psi _ j$ give rotational symmetry under $\mathrm{SO}(n)$. For $n\geq 3$, the stronger uniqueness theorem in [ ImagiJoyceOliveira2016 ] , Theorem 1.2, requires an embedded, exact, closed-as-a-subset Lagrangian expander asymptotic to two transverse planes at rate $\rho <2$. These hypotheses must not be dropped. No general stability claim is attached. The figure projects the $n=2$, $a_1=a_2=1$, $\psi _1=\psi _2=0$ member, evaluating its integrals numerically. title: 4.15 Two-convex Lagrangian graphical expanders
text:
Two-convexity here is a condition on a potential's Hessian, not hypersurface mean convexity. 9910637B58B3 (Expanders from homogeneous potentials) Let $n\geq 2$. Suppose $U_0:\mathbb R^ n	o \mathbb R$ is homogeneous of degree two, is $C^2$ away from the origin, and its Hessian eigenvalues obey \[  \lambda _ i+\lambda _ j\geq 0,\qquad 1+\lambda _ i\lambda _ j\geq 0\quad (i
e j), \qquad \prod _{i=1}^ n(1+\lambda _ i^2)^{-1/2}\geq \varepsilon _1>0.  \] Proposition 6.5 of [ TsaiTsuiWang2025 ] produces the unique solution in the stated continuous-initial-data, smooth-positive-time class of \[  u_ t=\sum _{i=1}^ n\arctan \lambda _ i(D^2u),\qquad u(x,0)=U_0(x),\qquad u(x,t)=t\, u(x/\sqrt t,1).  \] Then $L_ t=\{ (x,Du(x,t)):x\in \mathbb R^ n\} \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $t>0$, is self-expanding; $L_1$ satisfies $\vec H=X^\perp /2$. These are complete proper embedded graphs of dimension and codimension $n$, homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$, with one end. Hessian bounds persist and higher derivatives obey the estimates in Theorem 5.6. The initial cone is prescribed through the potential; no stronger asymptotic rate is asserted here. For a concrete nonquadratic seed, take $U_0(0)=0$ and \[  U_0(x)=- rac{x_1^2}{20}+ rac14\sum _{j=2}^ nx_ j^2 +10^{-4} rac{x_1^4}{|x|^2}\quad (x
e 0).  \] A direct differentiation bounds the operator norm of $D^2(x_1^4/|x|^2)$ by $38$. Thus one Hessian eigenvalue lies within $0.0038$ of $-0.1$, and the others within $0.0038$ of $0.5$. Both pair inequalities are strictly positive. This verifies the theorem's hypotheses while keeping the potential nonconvex. This formula describes initial data, not the positive-time expander.
