title: 4.18 Lee–Wang embedded quadric expanders
text: A1A5802C8577 (The expanding mixed-sign quadric family) For $n\geq 3$, $n/2<k<n$, and $S=2k-n$, set \[  Q_-=\left\{ x\in \mathbb R^ n:\sum _{j\leq k}x_ j^2-\sum _{j>k}x_ j^2=-2S\right\} ,\qquad X(x,s)=(e^{is}x_1,\ldots ,e^{is}x_ k,e^{-is}x_{k+1},\ldots ,e^{-is}x_ n).  \] On $(Q_-\times \mathbb R)/((x,s)\sim (-x,s+\pi ))$ this is a complete proper embedded Lagrangian in $\mathbb C^ n$, of dimension and codimension $n$. It satisfies $\vec H=X^\perp /2$, and $L_ t=\sqrt t\, X(Q_-\times \mathbb R)$ for $t>0$. This is an exact parametrization subject to one quadric constraint, not an ODE approximation. See [ LeeWang2010 ] , Propositions 2.1–2.2, with weights $+1$ and $-1$. The fiber is $\mathbb R^ k\times S^{n-k-1}$. The mapping-torus quotient is connected and has one end. If $n-k=1$, its two fiber components are exchanged by the gluing, and the total manifold is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ k\times S^1$, hence orientable. For $n-k\geq 2$ the fiber is connected, the antipodal monodromy must be retained, and the total manifold is orientable exactly when $n$ is even. In particular, the $n=3,k=2$ case is orientable: one must pass around the base twice to return to the same component. These topology statements are obtained from the quotient directly; the product and parity shorthand in the source's Proposition 2.2 requires this disconnected-fiber qualification. The family is noncompact and Hamiltonian stationary, with $SO(k)\times SO(n-k)$ and circle symmetries, and is asymptotic to the same cone as Example 2.50 . Its planar-coordinate quadric description gives polynomial volume growth and finite centered Gaussian area; this entry records no entropy value or stability result. No surface genus is assigned to these $n\geq 3$ examples. The source's weak continuation at $t=0$ is a separate varifold statement; the smooth time interval here is $t>0$. For the illustrated case $n=3$, $k=2$, the full expander has the global parametrization \[  F_ t(a,b,s)=\left(e^{is}a,e^{is}b,e^{-is}\sqrt{a^2+b^2+2t}\right), \qquad (a,b)\in \mathbb R^2,\quad s\in \mathbb R/(2\pi \mathbb Z),\quad t>0.  \] This parametrization is obtained directly from the unit-weight construction in [ LeeWang2010 ] , Theorem 1.1 and Section 2.2: one takes the positive component of the real quadric and a full circle of phases. The real slice, obtained at $s=0$ and $s=\pi $, consists of the two graphs \[  x_3=\pm \sqrt{r^2+2t},\qquad r=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}\geq 0.  \] Their tips are at $x_3=\pm \sqrt{2t}$. The figure compares $t=1/4,1,4$ with the singular cone limit $t=0$, using the same spatial scale and the fixed display cutoff $r\leq 3.2$. The complete slices are unbounded. These are exact two-dimensional slices of a three-dimensional flow in $\mathbb R^6$; they are not themselves mean curvature flows in $\mathbb R^3$. The circle direction explains why two real sheets do not mean two components of the expander. For a point $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ on the positive real sheet, the curve \[  \gamma _ x(s)=\left(e^{is}x_1,e^{is}x_2,e^{-is}x_3\right) =\cos (s)x+\sin (s)i(x_1,x_2,-x_3),\qquad 0\leq s\leq \pi ,  \] lies in $L_ t$ and joins $x$ to $-x$ on the other real sheet. It is a semicircle in a real two-plane in $\mathbb R^6$, since the two spanning vectors are orthogonal and have equal length. The circle-phase control follows this path at fixed time; only the time control changes the flow. If $n-k=1$, its two fiber components are exchanged by the gluing, and the total manifold is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ k\times S^1$, hence orientable. For $n-k\geq 2$ the fiber is connected, the antipodal monodromy must be retained, and the total manifold is orientable exactly when $n$ is even. section: 5.13 Minimal surfaces as stationary mean curvature flows
text: AC1C0D984A58 Every smooth minimal surface gives a static solution of mean curvature flow, and the same observation applies to minimal submanifolds in arbitrary codimension. Let $F_0:M^ n\to (N^{n+k},\bar g)$ be a smooth immersion without boundary, with $n\geq 2$, $k\geq 1$, and a fixed ambient metric. Write $\vec H$ for the trace of its second fundamental form. The time-independent family \[  F(p,t)=F_0(p),\qquad p\in M,\quad t\in \mathbb R,  \] satisfies the geometric mean curvature flow equation precisely when $F_0$ is minimal: \[  (\partial _ tF)^\perp =\vec H \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \vec H_{F_0}=0.  \] Thus every such minimal immersion is an eternal stationary flow; restricting time to $(-\infty ,T)$ also gives an ancient flow. No dilation, translation velocity, or preferred scale is required. Tangential reparametrizations can change the labels of points without changing the stationary geometry. Minimality and the geometry of the time slices. For a compactly supported normal variation $V$, supported away from any boundary, the first variation of area is \[  \delta \operatorname {Area}_{F_0}(V)=-\int _ M\langle \vec H,V\rangle \, d\mu .  \] For an infinite-area immersion this means the variation of area on a compact region containing the support. Minimality is therefore the critical-point equation for area. The first-variation argument and the stationary-flow observation are recorded for Euclidean hypersurfaces in [ Man11 ] , Proposition 1.2.1 and Sections 1.3–1.4, printed pp. 6–11 (supplied PDF pp. 19–24). The vector equation above gives the same conclusion in any fixed Riemannian ambient manifold. The flow retains the topology, embeddedness or self-intersections, completeness, properness, symmetries, and ends of the chosen minimal immersion. None of these properties follows merely from $\vec H=0$. In particular, both embedded and nonembedded immersed examples are allowed, and an immersion is not automatically nonembedded. For a surface in $\mathbb R^3$, minimality gives principal curvatures $\kappa _1+\kappa _2=0$ and hence $K=-\kappa _1^2\leq 0$; it does not force the surface to be flat. There is no positive-dimensional compact minimal immersion without boundary in Euclidean space. Indeed, for $F_0:M^ n\to \mathbb R^{n+k}$, \[  \Delta _ M F_0=\vec H,\qquad \Delta _ M|F_0|^2=2n+2\langle F_0,\vec H\rangle .  \] If $\vec H=0$ and $M$ were compact without boundary, integration would give $0=2n\operatorname {Vol}(M)$. This obstruction is specific to Euclidean space. Minimal surfaces in curved ambient manifolds are stationary for MCF in that ambient metric and are recorded separately below; their Euclidean mean curvature after an ambient embedding need not vanish. A minimal surface with boundary is also stationary in its interior, but a boundary-value flow must impose compatible boundary conditions, such as keeping its boundary fixed. Minimal graphs and affine planes. For a smooth hypersurface graph $F_0(x)=(x,u(x))$ over an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$, the stationary equation is the minimal-surface equation \[  \operatorname {div}\left(\frac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}\right)=0.  \] It is exactly the time-independent case of the graphical MCF equation \[  u_ t=\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}\, \operatorname {div}\left(\frac{Du}{\sqrt{1+|Du|^2}}\right);  \] see [ Man11 ] , Exercise 1.3.8, printed pp. 10–11. This is an elliptic characterization, not a closed formula for all minimal surfaces. An elementary exact example is any affine plane in $\mathbb R^3$: \[  F(u,v,t)=p+u e_1+v e_2,\qquad (u,v)\in \mathbb R^2,\quad t\in \mathbb R,  \] where $p\in \mathbb R^3$ and $e_1,e_2$ are orthonormal. It is complete, properly embedded, flat, noncompact, and topologically $\mathbb R^2$, with genus zero and one end. Unlike a plane solving the normalized shrinker equation, a stationary affine plane need not pass through the origin. The catenoid as an illustrated member of the class. For $a>0$ the exact parametrization \[  X(\theta ,s,t)=a(\cosh s\cos \theta ,\cosh s\sin \theta ,s), \quad \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z,\quad s\in \mathbb R,\quad t\in \mathbb R,  \] is independent of time and has $\vec H=0$. It is therefore an eternal stationary mean curvature flow in $\mathbb R^3$. Every time slice is a complete properly embedded noncompact rotational annulus, with two ends and a waist circle of radius $a$. Its metric and curvature are \[  g=a^2\cosh ^2s(d\theta ^2+ds^2),\qquad K=-\frac1{a^2\cosh ^4s},\qquad \int K\, dA=-4\pi .  \] The metric follows by differentiation, and the conformal curvature formula gives $K$ and its integral. The complete catenoid is unstable for compactly supported area variations: for a test function $f(s)$ independent of $\theta $, its second variation is \[  Q(f,f)=2\pi \int _{\mathbb R}\bigl ((f')^2-2\operatorname {sech}^2s\, f^2\bigr )\, ds.  \] Taking $f$ equal to one on $[-R,R]$, zero outside $[-2R,2R]$, and $|f'|\leq C/R$ makes this negative for large $R$. Each open half is a minimal graph over $r>a$, with $z=\pm a\operatorname {arcosh}(r/a)$, so it is stable for compactly supported variations in that half. These are minimal-area stability assertions, not a classification of dynamical stability under MCF. The supplied source also records the catenoid in [ Man11 ] , Remark 4.4.7, printed p. 105, supplied PDF p. 116. The interactive figure shows this particular minimal surface, with rotation and zoom on a fixed, truncated parameter window; it does not represent the full class of minimal surfaces. Chopp uses the bounded piece of this classical surface as a numerical benchmark in [ ChoppMinimal1993 ] , Section 4.1, pp. 86–87. In axial coordinates its exact profile is $r(z)=a\cosh (z/a)$, $-b\leq z\leq b$, with the two fixed boundary circles of radius $R=a\cosh (b/a)$. The test uses $a=0.4$ and $b\approx 0.277259$, giving $R\approx 0.5$. This is a fixed-boundary minimal-surface computation, not a new complete catenoid or a closed formula for the transient numerical evolution. The solver's artificial time and curvature conventions should not be identified with the normalized MCF time used elsewhere in this collection. Stationarity, stability, and Gaussian quantities. Being a critical point of area does not mean being an area minimizer or even stable. For a two-sided minimal hypersurface in Euclidean space, the second variation for a compactly supported scalar normal variation $f$ is \[  Q(f,f)=\int _ M\bigl (|\nabla f|^2-|A|^2f^2\bigr )\, d\mu .  \] An affine plane has $A=0$ and is stable for these variations, whereas the catenoid has the negative direction exhibited above. Both nevertheless remain exactly fixed under MCF when initialized at the minimal surface. Stability of perturbed flows requires its own hypotheses and is not asserted for this general class. For a stationary Euclidean immersion, each Gaussian integral and its entropy are constant in time whenever defined, because the immersion itself is fixed. This does not identify centered Gaussian area with entropy or imply their finiteness for every minimal immersion. For the multiplicity-one affine plane $P$ above, direct Gaussian integration gives \[  F_{x_0,\tau }(P)=\exp \left(-\frac{\operatorname {dist}(x_0,P)^2}{4\tau }\right), \qquad \lambda (P)=1,\qquad \tau >0.  \] Thus $F_{0,1}(P)=\exp (-\operatorname {dist}(0,P)^2/4)$ equals entropy only when $0\in P$. No value or uniform bound is recorded here for the general minimal-surface class. Euclidean Gaussian area and entropy are not assigned to intrinsic MCF in curved ambient manifolds. This entry concerns smooth minimal immersions; singular stationary varifolds require a weak-flow formulation and local mass hypotheses. Further stationary examples in this collection include the special Lagrangian Lawlor necks in 5.28 and the Su–Wood products in 5.37 . Their entries give the dimensions, parametrizations, and additional geometry of those particular families. section: 5.31 Mean curvature evolution of the Whitney sphere
text: 245DFF2BED27 (A collapsing Lagrangian immersed sphere) For $n\geq 2$, the initial Whitney immersion in $\mathbb R^{2n}=\mathbb C^ n$ is explicitly \[  F_0(x_1,\ldots ,x_{n+1}) =\frac{(x_1,x_1x_{n+1},\ldots ,x_ n,x_ nx_{n+1})}{1+x_{n+1}^2}, \qquad (x_1,\ldots ,x_{n+1})\in S^ n.  \] It is a compact Lagrangian immersion, of dimension and codimension $n$, with one transverse double image point at the origin coming from the two poles. It is complete and proper as an immersion of a compact domain, and it is not embedded. Its equivariance reduces the geometry to the planar initial profile \[  \gamma _0(u)=\left(\frac{\sin u}{1+\cos ^2u}, \frac{\sin u\cos u}{1+\cos ^2u}\right), \qquad u\in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z.  \] For $n\geq 2$ the profile evolution is the equivariant equation \[  (\partial _ t\gamma )^\perp =\vec k-(n-1)\frac{\gamma ^\perp }{|\gamma |^2},  \] interpreted by the smooth equivariant immersion at the double point. It is not ordinary planar curve shortening. The maximal smooth mean curvature flow $F_ t$, $t\in [0,T)$, remains Lagrangian and equivariant. It collapses to the origin in finite time, and its tangent flow there is a Lagrangian plane with multiplicity two. The Whitney sphere is not a self-similar solution. These statements are the special case stated in [ Viana18 ] , pp. 1–3, especially the result on p. 2 and Theorem 1.3 on p. 3. The formulas above specify the initial geometry and its reduced equation, not a closed expression for $F_ t$ at positive time. The illustration specializes to $n=2$. Write $\gamma _ t=a+ib$. A single right-hand lobe, from one preimage of the origin to the other, generates the immersed two-sphere by \[  F_ t(u,v)=(\gamma _ t(u)\cos v,\gamma _ t(u)\sin v)\in \mathbb C^2, \qquad v\in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z.  \] The circles at the two endpoints collapse to the two distinct poles of the domain, which have the same image at the origin. Using both antipodal lobes would cover the same sphere twice. The time sequence pairs this surface, linearly projected from $\mathbb R^4$ to $\mathbb R^3$, with its planar profile. At $t=0$ the geometry is exact; the positive-time frames are numerical approximations of the equivariant PDE for $n=2$, with $\partial _ tF=\vec H$ and the initial scale fixed above. They show $0\leq t\leq 0.09$ on a common spatial scale, with no normalization by an estimated extinction time. The computation stops before the singularity: $0.09$ is not asserted to equal $T$. The profile narrows and contracts rather than shrinking by a single scale factor. Its double point remains at the origin; further overlaps in the surface projection need not be intersections in $\mathbb R^4$. title: 5.14 Rotational degenerate neckpinch solutions
text: 922034E946EB (Angenent–Velázquez type-II singularities) Let $n\geq 2$, let $m\geq 3$ be odd, and let $K>0$. Choose a compact rotational target hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, smooth away from a cusp at the origin, whose radius satisfies $u_*(x)\sim \sqrt K\, x^{m/2}$ as $x\downarrow 0$ and whose other tip closes smoothly. Angenent and Velázquez construct smooth compact rotational mean curvature flows \[  M_ t=\{ (x,u(x,t)\omega ):a(t)\leq x\leq b(t),\  \omega \in S^{n-1}\} , \qquad t_0<t<T,  \] with smooth caps and positive radius between them. Each regular slice is an embedded sphere, hence complete and proper. The constructed flows remain close to the chosen target outside a small neighborhood of the origin as the construction interval is shortened. They are not supplied as ancient solutions or as solitons, and no closed formula for $u(x,t)$ is given. Set $\xi _*=(2(n-1)/K)^{1/m}$. At the left tip, \[  a(t)=-(\xi _*+o(1))(T-t)^{1/m},\qquad |\vec H|_{\rm tip}(t)=\left(\frac{\xi _*}{m}+o(1)\right)(T-t)^{1/m-1}.  \] Here the curvature coefficient is for the trace mean curvature, equivalently the magnitude $|\vec H|$ at this convex tip. Rotational smoothness makes the $n$ principal curvatures equal at the tip, so $|A|_{\rm tip}=|\vec H|_{\rm tip}/\sqrt n$. The maximum of $|A|$ is attained there; its blow-up rate is type II. The parabolic rescalings at the origin converge smoothly on compact sets to $S^{n-1}_{\sqrt{2(n-1)}}\times \mathbb R$, whereas rescaling about the tip by $A_{\max }(t)=\max _{M_ t}|A|$ yields the rotational translating bowl with tip $|A|=1$. This last normalization has translation speed $\sqrt n$; rescaling instead by $|\vec H|_{\rm tip}$ gives the speed-one bowl. Under the intermediate scaling $x\mapsto x/(T-t)^{1/m}$ and $r\mapsto r/(T-t)^{1/2}$, the limiting profile is \[  r=\sqrt{2(n-1)+Kx^ m},\qquad x\geq -\xi _*.  \] This last expression is an asymptotic limiting profile, not an exact formula for the evolving compact hypersurface. Source: [ AV97 ] , Introduction, items 1–5, printed pp. 16–17, supplied PDF pp. 2–3; the construction is justified in Sections 3–7. The even-$m$ modifications and the formal $m=2$ discussion are not included in this entry. The illustration selects $n=2$, $m=3$, $K=1$, and writes $s=T-t$. Its time sequence uses one spatial scale to show the left tip approaching the origin while the outer cap persists; the final cusp target is not a smooth time slice. For the profile near the origin, item 5 of the Introduction gives \[  \frac{u(y\sqrt{s},T-s)}{\sqrt{s}} =\sqrt{2}+\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2\sqrt{2}}(y^3-6y)+o(\sqrt{s})  \] on bounded $y$ intervals. This leading Hermite correction explains the small bulge and neck in the cylindrical region. The rotatable compact slices blend the asymptotic profiles with a numerically integrated bowl cap and a chosen outer cap: they are illustrative schematics, not a computed solution of the compact MCF initial-value problem, and their displayed times carry no certified finite-time accuracy. Separate views compare the meridians and the three blow-up limits; the intermediate view uses unequal axial and radial scaling. The construction does not classify all type-II singularities or impose global convexity on every allowed target. 922034E946EB (Angenent–Velázquez type-II singularities) Let $n\geq 2$, let $m\geq 3$ be odd, and let $K>0$. Choose a compact rotational target hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, smooth away from a cusp at the origin, whose radius satisfies $u_*(x)\sim \sqrt K\, x^{m/2}$ as $x\downarrow 0$ and whose other tip closes smoothly. Angenent and Velázquez construct smooth compact rotational mean curvature flows \[  M_ t=\{ (x,u(x,t)\omega ):a(t)\leq x\leq b(t),\  \omega \in S^{n-1}\} , \qquad t_0<t<T,  \] with smooth caps and positive radius between them. Each regular slice is an embedded sphere, hence complete and proper. The constructed flows remain close to the chosen target outside a small neighborhood of the origin as the construction interval is shortened. They are not supplied as ancient solutions or as solitons, and no closed formula for $u(x,t)$ is given. Set $\xi _*=(2(n-1)/K)^{1/m}$. At the left tip, \[  a(t)=-(\xi _*+o(1))(T-t)^{1/m},\qquad |\vec H|_{\rm tip}(t)=\left(\frac{\xi _*}{m}+o(1)\right)(T-t)^{1/m-1}.  \] Here the curvature coefficient is for the trace mean curvature, equivalently the magnitude $|\vec H|$ at this convex tip. Rotational smoothness makes the $n$ principal curvatures equal at the tip, so $|A|_{\rm tip}=|\vec H|_{\rm tip}/\sqrt n$. The maximum of $|A|$ is attained there; its blow-up rate is type II. The parabolic rescalings at the origin converge smoothly on compact sets to $S^{n-1}_{\sqrt{2(n-1)}}\times \mathbb R$, whereas rescaling about the tip by $A_{\max }(t)=\max _{M_ t}|A|$ yields the rotational translating bowl with tip $|A|=1$. This last normalization has translation speed $\sqrt n$; rescaling instead by $|\vec H|_{\rm tip}$ gives the speed-one bowl. The even-$m$ modifications and the formal $m=2$ discussion are not included in this entry. The illustration selects $n=2$, $m=3$, $K=1$, and writes $s=T-t$. Its time sequence uses one spatial scale to show the left tip approaching the origin while the outer cap persists; the final cusp target is not a smooth time slice. For the profile near the origin, item 5 of the Introduction gives \[  \frac{u(y\sqrt{s},T-s)}{\sqrt{s}} =\sqrt{2}+\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2\sqrt{2}}(y^3-6y)+o(\sqrt{s})  \] on bounded $y$ intervals. Separate views compare the meridians and the three blow-up limits; the intermediate view uses unequal axial and radial scaling. The construction does not classify all type-II singularities or impose global convexity on every allowed target.

title: 5.5 The Angenent oval as an explicit ancient flow

section: 5.5 The Angenent oval as an explicit ancient flow
text: B008243C5D96 (The ancient paperclip curve) With the speed-one curve-shortening convention, the exact implicit equation \[  \Gamma _ t=\{ (x,y)\in \mathbb R^2:|x|<\pi /2,\  e^ t\cosh y=\cos x\} , \qquad -\infty <t<0,  \] defines the Angenent oval. Equivalently, its two graph branches are \[  y=\pm \operatorname {arcosh}(e^{-t}\cos x), \qquad |x|\leq \arccos (e^ t).  \] Their endpoints join smoothly as a curve, even though those graph charts cease to be regular there. This is an exact implicit formula, rather than a single global graph parametrization. It is recorded in [ BV11 ] , Section 3.1, equation (14), p. 7. Every time slice is a smooth compact embedded strictly convex curve, hence complete and proper, with topology $S^1$ and reflection symmetries across both coordinate axes. It shrinks to the origin at time zero but changes shape and is not a soliton. Its enclosed area is $-2\pi t$, and \[  \kappa _{\max }=(1-e^{2t})^{-1/2},\qquad \kappa _{\min }=e^ t(1-e^{2t})^{-1/2}.  \] The rescaling $(-t)^{-1/2}\Gamma _ t$ converges smoothly to the radius-$\sqrt2$ circle at extinction. As $t\to -\infty $, translating its upper and lower branches to keep their tips fixed gives the two oppositely directed grim-reaper profiles, locally in $|x|<\pi /2$. These limits can be read from the implicit equation: near extinction its quadratic expansion gives $x^2+y^2\sim -2t$, and subtracting the upper tip height gives the limiting graph $\log \cos x$ as $t\to -\infty $. The time slider plots the exact implicit curve for $-5\leq t\leq -0.1$ on a fixed spatial scale. title: 5.29 Ancient torus curves in higher codimension (D. J. Altschuler–S. J. Altschuler–Angenent–Wu, 2012; Stryker–Sun, 2019)

section: 5.29 Ancient torus curves in higher codimension (D. J. Altschuler–S. J. Altschuler–Angenent–Wu, 2012; Stryker–Sun, 2019)
text: D28FAF32B556 (Compact ancient torus curves) Fix $m\geq 2$ and integers $1=k_1<k_2<\cdots <k_ m$. For $t<0$, let $r(t)>0$ be the unique solution of \[  \sum _{j=1}^ m r(t)^{2k_ j^2}=-2t.  \] Then the exact parametrization \[  \gamma _ t(\theta )= \bigl (r(t)^{k_1^2}\cos (k_1\theta ),r(t)^{k_1^2}\sin (k_1\theta ), \ldots ,r(t)^{k_ m^2}\cos (k_ m\theta ),r(t)^{k_ m^2}\sin (k_ m\theta )\bigr ), \qquad \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z,  \] is an ancient curve-shortening flow in $\mathbb R^{2m}$. Its scale is specified by an exact implicit equation; no elementary inverse in time is required. Equivalently, \[  r'=-\frac{r}{\sum _ j k_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}}.  \] Each time slice is a compact smooth embedded circle, hence complete and proper, with no ends and codimension $2m-1$. Embeddedness follows directly from $k_1=1$, because the first two coordinates already determine $\theta $. The name refers to a curve lying on a product of circles, not to a two-dimensional torus. It spans $\mathbb R^{2m}$, has a one-parameter simultaneous rotational symmetry, and is non-self-similar when $m\geq 2$ because the ratios of its different coordinate radii change with time. The rescaled curves $(-t)^{-1/2}\gamma _ t$ tend to the radius-$\sqrt2$ circle with multiplicity $k_ m$ as $t\to -\infty $, and with multiplicity one as $t\uparrow 0$. Stryker–Sun prove \[  \sup _{t<0}\lambda (\gamma _ t)=k_ m\lambda (S^1) =k_ m\sqrt{\frac{2\pi }{e}},  \] which also bounds the entropy of every time slice. This is a supremum over time, not a formula for the entropy at each finite time. For the fixed center and Gaussian scale, direct integration gives \[  F_{0,1}(\gamma _ t)=\sqrt\pi \left(\sum _ j k_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}\right)^{1/2}e^{t/2}.  \] Indeed, $|\gamma _ t|^2=-2t$ and $|\partial _\theta \gamma _ t|^2=\sum _ jk_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}$. The centered Gaussian area is distinct from the supremum defining $\lambda $. Source: [ SS19 ] , equation (2.1), Propositions 2.1–2.2, Corollary 2.3, and Theorem A.1, PDF pp. 3–5 and 8–9. The general source formula allows $k_1>1$; if the frequencies have common divisor $d>1$, that parametrization is a $d$-fold cover and its mass counts multiplicity. The embedded subfamily above avoids this ambiguity. The construction was already present in [ AAAW13 ] , Section 3, equations (11)–(14), PDF pp. 8–9, as acknowledged in [ SS19 ] , Remark 1.3. The interactive figure uses $(k_1,k_2)=(1,2)$ in $\mathbb R^4$. Its three-coordinate display is a projection, with time and fourth-coordinate rotation controls. title: 5.16 Eternal shrinking helices (D. J. Altschuler–S. J. Altschuler–Angenent–Wu, 2012; Stryker–Sun, 2019)
search_title: Eternal shrinking helices (D. J. Altschuler–S. J. Altschuler–Angenent–Wu, 2012; Stryker–Sun, 2019)
section: 5.16 Eternal shrinking helices (D. J. Altschuler–S. J. Altschuler–Angenent–Wu, 2012; Stryker–Sun, 2019)
text: 1EF23C4EFFC0 (Helical curve-shortening flows) Fix $m\geq 1$ and integers $1\leq k_1<\cdots <k_ m$. Let $r(t)>0$, $t\in \mathbb R$, solve the exact implicit equation \[  \log r(t)+\frac12\sum _{j=1}^ m r(t)^{2k_ j^2}=\frac m2-t.  \] The choice of constant makes $r(0)=1$. Then \[  \Gamma _ t(s)= \bigl (r^{k_1^2}\cos (k_1s),r^{k_1^2}\sin (k_1s),\ldots , r^{k_ m^2}\cos (k_ ms),r^{k_ m^2}\sin (k_ ms),s\bigr ), \qquad s\in \mathbb R,  \] is an eternal curve-shortening flow in $\mathbb R^{2m+1}$. In the simplest case $m=1$, $k_1=1$, it is the three-dimensional helix \[  \Gamma _ t(s)=(r(t)\cos s,r(t)\sin s,s),\qquad \log r(t)+r(t)^2/2=1/2-t.  \] These are exact parametrizations with an implicitly determined time scale, not numerical ODE profiles. The ordinary differential equation is \[  r'=-\frac{r}{1+\sum _ j k_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}}.  \] The last coordinate makes every time slice a proper embedding of $\mathbb R$, and the induced metric is $(1+\sum _ jk_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2})ds^2$, so it is complete. It is noncompact with two ends and codimension $2m$, and it spans the stated ambient space. Simultaneous rotations together with translation along the last coordinate give its screw symmetry. Its radius decreases to zero as $t\to +\infty $, giving local smooth convergence to the axis, while $r(t)\to \infty $ as $t\to -\infty $. At any fixed finite time the ends continue winding; they are not asymptotic to the axis as $|s|\to \infty $. Proposition 2.7 of [ SS19 ] proves \[  \sup _{t\in \mathbb R}\lambda (\Gamma _ t)=+\infty .  \] This concerns the entire time family and does not say that every individual slice has infinite entropy. In fact, a direct calculation gives the exact fixed-time entropy below. Set $B=\sum _ jr^{2k_ j^2}$ and $D=\sum _ jk_ j^2r^{2k_ j^2}$. Direct Gaussian integration, using $|\Gamma _ t(s)|^2=B+s^2$, gives the exact centered value \[  F_{0,1}(\Gamma _ t)=\sqrt{1+D}\, e^{-B/4}; \qquad F_{0,1}(\Gamma _ t)=\sqrt{1+r^2}\, e^{-r^2/4} \quad \hbox{when }m=k_1=1.  \] For completeness, the same calculation at arbitrary Gaussian scale gives \[  \lambda (\Gamma _ t)=\sqrt{1+D(t)}.  \] Indeed, for a center $(a,z_0)\in \mathbb R^{2m}\times \mathbb R$, dropping the nonnegative squared distance in the first $2m$ coordinates bounds $F_{(a,z_0),\tau }$ by $(4\pi \tau )^{-1/2}\sqrt{1+D}\int _{\mathbb R}e^{-(s-z_0)^2/(4\tau )}\, ds=\sqrt{1+D}$. At the origin, $F_{0,\tau }=\sqrt{1+D}e^{-B/(4\tau )}$ tends to this upper bound as $\tau \to \infty $. Thus every finite-time helix has finite entropy, while the time supremum is infinite. This is a direct integration, additional to the cited time-supremum result. Source: [ SS19 ] , equation (2.6), Propositions 2.6–2.7, and Theorem A.2, PDF pp. 6–7 and 9; see also [ AAAW13 ] , Section 3, PDF pp. 8–10. The interactive three-dimensional figure uses the simplest exact helix, with a time slider and the displayed range $-5\pi /2\leq s\leq 5\pi /2$. section: 5.27 Immortal annuli converging to a double plane
text: A50018836027 (Chen–Sun's noncompact multiplicity-two limit) Chen and Sun construct a nonstatic immortal mean curvature flow $M_ t\subset \mathbb R^3$, $t\in [0,\infty )$, smooth for $t>0$, of connected embedded rotational surfaces. It is also symmetric across the limiting plane. Each positive-time slice consists of two increasing radial graphs joined smoothly at a neck of radius $a(t)>0$: \[  M_ t=\{ (\rho \cos \theta ,\rho \sin \theta ,\pm f(\rho ,t)): \rho \geq a(t),\  \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z\} .  \] This is a description of the constructed PDE solution, not an explicit formula for $f$. Away from the neck its upper graph satisfies \[  f_ t=\frac{f_{\rho \rho }}{1+f_\rho ^2}+\frac{f_\rho }{\rho }.  \] Near the neck, the inverse graph $\rho =u(z,t)$ instead satisfies \[  u_ t=\frac{u_{zz}}{1+u_ z^2}-\frac1u,\qquad u_ z(0,t)=0.  \] The proof selects a critical initial surface by interpolation among rotational surfaces in finite cylinders and then takes a limit as the cylinder radius tends to infinity. Its initial trace is locally Lipschitz; choosing any positive time as the initial time gives an entirely smooth immortal flow. No closed formula, canonical parameter value, or uniqueness of the constructed critical flow is supplied. The two graphical ends and the smooth connecting neck give topology $S^1\times \mathbb R$: genus zero and two ends. Properness follows from the graphs escaping to infinite radius; the smooth connected surface is complete. It remains in a fixed slab, and the two ends stay asymptotic to their original parallel planes. The neck radius tends to zero only as $t\to \infty $. On compact regions the flow converges to the middle plane with multiplicity two; the two sheets converge smoothly away from the origin. The convergence is not uniform over the entire noncompact surface. This is an infinite-time limit of the unrescaled flow, not a multiplicity-two finite-time tangent flow of a closed embedded surface. Source: [ CS26R3 ] , Theorems 1.1 and 4.13, Section 1.1, equation (2.5), Proposition 4.6 and Remark 4.7, and Appendix A, arXiv v3 PDF pp. 1, 3, 6, 23–24, and 27–28. The topology and properness statements above are direct consequences of the source's two-graph parametrization. The paper gives no exact entropy or fixed-center Gaussian-area value for this constructed family. The interactive picture compares ordered finite-time stages and a separate infinite-time limit at a fixed viewing scale. A cutaway exposes the connecting neck; the compressed radial profile records the fixed far-end heights. title: 5.44 Immortal compact flows converging to a double sphere

section: 5.44 Immortal compact flows converging to a double sphere
text: 225751B3C7E8 (Chen–Sun's product-manifold construction) For each $n\geq 2$, there is a smooth connected embedded immortal mean curvature flow of compact hypersurfaces in the product manifold \[  (S^ n\times [-1,1],\  g_{S^ n}+dy^2),  \] where $S^ n$ has unit round radius. The flow is defined for all $t\geq 0$ and is nonstatic. Its hypersurface dimension is $n$ and its codimension in this ambient manifold is one. The construction stays in the smaller band $|y|\leq 1/(2n)$, so the same flow is contained in $S^ n\times \mathbb R$; it can also be placed in the closed product $S^ n\times (\mathbb R/4\mathbb Z)$ without changing the metric near the flow. There is no free boundary on $y=\pm 1$. The solution is invariant under rotations of the sphere about its polar axis, reflection $y\mapsto -y$, and reflection across the sphere's equator. A closed profile $\sigma \mapsto (x(\sigma ,t),y(\sigma ,t))$ in $(0,\pi )\times \mathbb R$ generates it by \[  (\sigma ,\omega )\longmapsto (\cos x(\sigma ,t),\sin x(\sigma ,t)\, \omega ,y(\sigma ,t)), \qquad \sigma \in S^1,\quad \omega \in S^{n-1}.  \] The profile avoids both axes at every finite time, so this parametrization directly gives topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$. Thus for $n=2$ the surfaces are genus-one tori with no ends. All slices are complete and proper by compactness. This is a topological deduction from the construction, not an assertion that the source states a separate topology theorem. No closed time-dependent profile is supplied. Its upper half can be described using the solution of \[  v_ t=\frac{v_{xx}}{1+v_ x^2}+(n-1)\cot x\, v_ x, \qquad v_ x(\pi /2,t)=0,  \] with an inverse graph near each neck, governed by \[  u_ t=\frac{u_{yy}}{1+u_ y^2}-(n-1)\cot u, \qquad u_ y(0,t)=0.  \] An interpolation argument selects an immortal solution. As $t\to \infty $, it converges to the stable minimal slice $S^ n\times \{ 0\} $ with multiplicity two. Away from the north and south poles, the two sheets converge smoothly; the two necks collapse only at infinite time. Source: [ CS25Man ] , Theorems 1.1, 3.12, and 3.17, Section 2.1, Definition 3.10 and Lemma 3.11, and Section 3.3, arXiv v2 PDF pp. 1–4 and 11–15. Euclidean Gaussian area and Colding–Minicozzi entropy are not assigned to this intrinsic manifold flow; the cited paper gives no such invariant for these examples. In particular, its isometric embedding into $\mathbb R^{n+2}$ is not an unforced Euclidean mean curvature flow. The picture pairs three ordered finite-time stages with the infinite-time limit and their orbit-space profiles. title: 5.18 Compact noncollapsed convex ancient ovals (Haslhofer–Hershkovits, 2013)
text: 56D296501918 For $n\geq 2$ and every $1\leq j\leq n-1$, Haslhofer–Hershkovits construct an ancient hypersurface flow $M_ t\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $-\infty <t<0$, with compact strictly convex embedded slices. Each slice is diffeomorphic to $S^ n$, hence complete and proper with no ends. The construction has $O(j+1)\times O(n-j)$ symmetry and is uniformly Andrews noncollapsed. It is not self-similar and becomes round at extinction. Under backward parabolic blow-down, \[  \lambda ^{-1}M_{\lambda ^2t}\longrightarrow S^ j(\sqrt{2j|t|})\times \mathbb R^{n-j}\quad (\lambda \to \infty ).  \] The tip rescalings selected in Claim 3.5 of [ HH13 ] approach $\mathrm{Bowl}^{j+1}\times \mathbb R^{n-j-1}$, with the bowl normalized to unit tip curvature. Rescaled diameter is unbounded backward in time and curvature decay is type II. No closed formula or uniqueness follows from this construction. Gaussian area and entropy are finite for each compact slice; no fixed slice value is evaluated here. Source: [ HH13 ] , Theorem 1.1 and Section 3. Huisken–Sinestrari's Theorem 3.2 in [ HS14 ] shows why the hypothesis $h_{ij}\geq \varepsilon H g_{ij}$ with one $\varepsilon >0$ for all ancient times cannot hold for these nonspherical ovals: a closed convex ancient flow with that uniform pinching is a shrinking sphere. The illustration specializes to $n=2$, $j=1$. It numerically evolves the boundary of the Minkowski sum of a unit ball and an ellipsoid with semiaxes $(8,1/2,1/2)$, using rotational mean curvature flow. This is a finite smooth convex seed inspired by the long capped cylinders in Section 3, not a closed formula for the ancient oval. Extinction is shifted to $t=0$, and parabolic scaling makes the axial-to-equatorial radius ratio equal to $2$ at $t=-1$. The slider samples $-1000\leq t\leq -0.001$. Original size shows contraction at a fixed spatial scale. The default view shows $(-t)^{-1/2}M_ t$: the backward central limit is the cylinder of radius $\sqrt2$, while the extinction limit is the sphere of radius $2$. The right-tip view instead translates the tip to the origin and multiplies lengths by its mean curvature; the dashed comparison is a numerically integrated unit-speed bowl. These are different rescalings. title: 5.21 The eternal reapernoid

8EACFCA7AE0F For every $n\geq 2$, Mramor–Payne construct an eternal embedded hypersurface flow $M_ t\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $t\in \mathbb R$, on the outside of a rotational minimal catenoid. It is $O(n)	imes O(1)$ invariant, mean convex after a choice of orientation, nonconvex, and has uniformly bounded curvature. Backward in time it converges smoothly and uniformly to that catenoid; forward in time its distance from the rotation axis tends to infinity. It is not a translator or another soliton. The rotational graphical construction gives complete proper noncompact slices with topology $S^{n-1}	imes \mathbb R$ and two ends. For $n=2$ these are annuli in $\mathbb R^3$. In that dimension the pointed forward profile limit is a line and curvature tends to zero. For $n\geq 3$, recentered meridians converge instead to a grim reaper with the same width as the higher-dimensional catenoid. These are pointed profile limits, not a claim that the unshifted surfaces converge globally to a fixed grim cylinder. Source: [ MP19 ] , Theorem 1.3, pp. 4–5, and Section 4. The scale of the limiting catenoid is free; no explicit time-dependent profile, full uniqueness statement, or entropy value is recorded. The figure uses numerical solutions of the rotational evolution equation (2.7), rather than dilating a fixed catenoid. u $ points outward. The convexity of the meridian does not make the hypersurface convex: its meridional and rotational principal curvatures have opposite signs. title: 5.34 Ancient stacked pancakes
text: 1A2B6DF32B79 For each $n\geq 3$, Mramor–Yudowitz construct a smooth ancient flow of closed embedded hypersurfaces $M_ t^ n\subset \mathbb R^{n+1}$ for $t\in (-\infty ,0]$. The slices are nonconvex, contained in a fixed slab, and $O(n)\times O(1)$ invariant. Their rotational radius profile is a graph over the axis with two local maxima separated by one local minimum. Topologically this is two lobes joined by one neck, giving $S^ n$; compactness gives completeness, properness, and zero ends. The endpoint $t=0$ is a regular chosen time, not an asserted extinction time. The theorem does not establish this construction for $n=2$, so the lowest ambient dimension is four. It also does not prove a precise backward decomposition into two separate ancient pancakes and a catenoid; the authors explicitly distinguish this motivation from their result. Existence uses a continuity and compactness argument. No closed formula, uniqueness, stability result, or uniform ancient entropy value is recorded. Each compact slice has finite entropy and Gaussian area. Source: [ MY26 ] , Theorem 1.1, Figure 1, and Sections 2.2–3.1 of arXiv v3. To read the pictures, write a rotational slice as $(u(x,t)\omega ,x)$, where $\omega \in S^{n-1}$ and $a(t)<x<b(t)$ is the axial coordinate. The positive radius $u$ has two maxima and a central neck minimum; it vanishes at the two poles. The first picture shows a schematic three-dimensional linear section, with a removable display cutaway exposing the neck. The second shows the meridian and a fixed containing slab. title: 5.10 Compact nonconvex ancient spiral curves
text: 505A2B69BD4F Zhang–Olson–Khan–Angenent construct compact embedded ancient curve-shortening flows $C_ t\subset \mathbb R^2$, $t<0$, whose distant past follows a truncated rotating Yin–Yang spiral closed by a small grim-reaper-shaped cap. They are smooth simple closed curves, hence complete and proper, with no ends. They are nonconvex in the ancient regime and are neither shrinking circles nor ancient paperclips. No assertion of nonconvexity through a later maximal continuation is needed here. The limiting rotating model has angular speed one. Its radial expansion $\mathcal R(\theta )=\sqrt{2\theta }+O(\theta ^{-3/2})$ is asymptotic, not a formula for the constructed ancient curve. If $\Omega (t)$ is the paper's truncated spiral region and $\Lambda (t)$ is the enclosed ancient region, the Main Theorem proves \[  |\Lambda (t)\mathbin {\triangle }\Omega (t)|\leq C_\delta |t|^{-1+\delta }\qquad (t\to -\infty )  \] for each $\delta >0$. This is an area estimate, not an exact pointwise parametrization. Gaussian area and entropy are finite at each compact slice; no uniform ancient bound is assigned. Source: [ ZOKA23 ] , Main Theorem and equations (1.1)–(1.3), pp. 1–3, and Appendix A. No uniqueness is claimed. The source also credits Charyyev's independent construction. The figure samples the asymptotic construction at $t=-24,-18,-12,-8$ on a common spatial scale. Its blue arms solve the rotating-soliton ODE numerically; the orange cap uses the corrected grim-reaper ansatz in Section 2. These are model snapshots, not a numerical solution of the ancient evolution equation or an illustration of extinction. To read the motion, write $E(\theta )=(\cos \theta ,\sin \theta )$ and $J(x,y)=(-y,x)$. The two arms are \[  Y_\pm (\theta ,t)=\mathcal R(\theta -t\pm \pi /2)E(\theta ), \qquad \theta -t\pm \pi /2>\pi /2,  \] truncated near $\theta =-t$. Here $\mathcal R$ is the Appendix A solution of \[  \tfrac 12\mathcal R^2-\theta +\arctan (\mathcal R'/\mathcal R)=0, \qquad \theta >\pi /2,  \] with $\mathcal R\downarrow 0$ as $\theta \downarrow \pi /2$. At a fixed point of the unrotated model the arms rotate counterclockwise with speed one. The cap center instead follows $R(t)E(-t)$, where $R(t)=\mathcal R(-2t)\sim 2\sqrt{-t}$, so it moves clockwise and inward. Its leading width is $\pi /R(t)$. The inset uses $X=e^{-tJ}[(R(t),0)+R(t)^{-1}(u,v)]$; its dashed reference is the leading grim reaper \[  G(p)=(-\arcsin (\tanh p),-\log \cosh p),\qquad p\in \mathbb R.  \] The orange curve includes the paper's normal correction $(-4t)^{-1}F(p)JG'(p)$, equations (2.19)–(2.21), and a smooth interpolation to the arms. text: B7D6B1E7217F Choose monotonically ordered heights $a_0<a_1<\cdots <a_ m$ and horizontal shifts $C_1,\ldots ,C_ m$. Angenent–You construct embedded eternal planar curve-shortening flows which for sufficiently negative time are assembled asymptotically from alternating grim reapers on consecutive strips. To record a definite nontrivial subfamily, take $m=3$. With $v_ k=\pi /(a_ k-a_{k-1})$, the separate asymptotic models are \[  x=C_ k+(-1)^ k\left[-v_ k^{-1}\log \sin (v_ k(y-a_{k-1}))+v_ kt\right], \qquad a_{k-1}<y<a_ k.  \] This formula describes the model translators, not the glued eternal solution. The actual flow is a graph $x=u(y,t)$ on $a_0<y<a_3$, exists for every $t\in \mathbb R$, and is complete, properly embedded and noncompact, with topology $\mathbb R$ and two ends asymptotic to the outer horizontal lines. The two-end and properness statements follow from this graphical description and the outer asymptotes. Curvature changes sign in the nontrivial chain; total absolute curvature is uniformly bounded. There is no closed formula for $u$; the classification and flow entropy are qualified below. Source: [ AY18 ] , equation (3), Section 3.1 and Lemmas 3.8–3.10, pp. 2 and 8–13. The paper also constructs immersed ancient chains; those are not being labeled embedded by this selected case. The illustration uses $a_ k=k\pi $ and $C_ k=0$, so that the three model tips have horizontal velocities $-1,+1,-1$. It shows a numerical finite-start approximation: smoothly joined reapers at $t=-10$ are evolved by curve shortening, and slices from $t=-6$ to $t=9$ are displayed at the same spatial scale. The outer ends are truncated far outside the viewing window. The joins follow the construction in Section 3.2 and Figure 10, using the orientation of equation (3) and Figure 9. This computation is not a closed formula or a certified approximation of the eternal limit; the later shapes are numerical observations, not an additional asymptotic theorem. In particular, $t=0$ is not an extinction time. Corollary 1.5 records flow entropy $m+1$ for the $m$-reaper family; thus the selected $m=3$ case has flow entropy four. This does not identify the entropy or centered Gaussian area of an individual slice with four. title: 5.28 Stationary special Lagrangian necks
text: Lawlor necks are the stationary endpoint of the Lagrangian neck construction. 263868E061E7 (Stationary special Lagrangian necks) For $n\geq 2$, $a_ j>0$, and phases $\psi _ j\in \mathbb R$, define \[  P_0(y)=\frac{\prod _{j=1}^ n(1+a_ jy^2)-1}{y^2},\quad P_0(0)=\sum _ ja_ j,\quad \phi _ j(y)=\psi _ j+\int _0^ y\frac{dt}{(a_ j^{-1}+t^2)\sqrt{P_0(t)}}.  \] The map \[  X(x,y)=\left(x_ j\sqrt{a_ j^{-1}+y^2}e^{i\phi _ j(y)}\right)_{j=1}^ n, \qquad (x,y)\in \mathbb S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R,  \] parametrizes a complete proper embedded special Lagrangian of dimension and codimension $n$. Its constant flow $L_ t=X(\mathbb S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R)$ is eternal, $t\in \mathbb R$, since $\vec H=0$. This is the $\alpha =0$ case of [ JoyceLeeTsui2010 ] , Theorems C–D, credited there to Lawlor. It has two planar ends and topology $\mathbb S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$; in $\mathbb C^2$ it is an annulus. The positive characteristic angles sum to $\pi $. They determine a neck up to scale, and equal $a_ j$ give the rotational subfamily after a unitary change of coordinates. Calibration makes the neck area-minimizing for compactly supported competitors with the same boundary, hence stable for compactly supported variations. For $n\geq 3$, [ ImagiJoyceOliveira2016 ] , Theorem 1.1, classifies closed-as-subsets, embedded, exact, asymptotically conical special Lagrangians with two transverse planar asymptotes and rate $\rho <0$, up to the specified special unitary rotation. text: The ambient space here is a Riemannian two-sphere, not Euclidean space. CC2635F97DC0 (A circle of limiting geodesics) For every $C^\infty $ neighborhood of the round metric on $\mathbb S^2$, [ AryanLee2026 ] , Theorem 5.1, constructs a smooth antipodally invariant metric $g$ in that neighborhood and a smooth simple closed curve whose curve-shortening flow \[  \partial _ t\gamma =\kappa _ gN_ g,\qquad t\in [0,\infty ),  \] stays embedded for all time. There is an embedded circle $Z\subset \mathbb {RP}^2$ and a smooth injective family $\Gamma :Z\to \mathcal E^\infty (\mathbb S^2)$ of simple closed $g$-geodesics, all of the same length, such that \[  \omega _{C^\infty }(\gamma )=\{ \Gamma (z):z\in Z\} .  \] Convergence is convergence of unparametrized embedded curves, or smooth convergence after reparametrization. In particular there is no unique limiting geodesic. Each regular slice is a compact complete proper embedded circle, of dimension one and codimension one in $(\mathbb S^2,g)$, with no ends. The construction uses a prescribed length function and a spiraling slow mode, not a closed time-dependent formula. It does not assert rotational symmetry or stability of the evolving curve. The diagram is a schematic in parameter space; it is not a curve-shortening simulation on the round sphere. Euclidean Gaussian area and entropy are inapplicable to this intrinsic ambient flow. text: These compact flows live in a flat complex torus, which is kept in the Riemannian-ambient group. 2DFF070BC43F (Immortal Lagrangian connected sums) Let $m\geq 3$ and let $X_1,X_2$ be special Lagrangian $m$-tori of the same phase in the flat Calabi–Yau torus $\mathbb C^ m/\Gamma $. Assume they intersect transversely at exactly one point, with tangent planes satisfying the Lawlor angle criterion (a type-one intersection). By [ SuTsaiWood2026 ] , the Main Theorem, Theorem 9.1, Proposition 9.5, and Corollary 9.6, a sufficiently small Lawlor-neck desingularization can be chosen to start a smooth embedded immortal Lagrangian flow $N_ t$. After translating the initial time, take $t\geq 0$. Every finite-time slice is a compact complete proper embedded $m$-manifold of codimension $m$, with topology $\mathbb T^ m\mathbin {\# }\mathbb T^ m$ and no ends. As $t\to \infty $, the flow converges smoothly away from the intersection point to $X_1\cup X_2$. Its neck scale and curvature satisfy, for sufficiently large $t$, \[  c\, t^{-1/(m-2)}\leq \varepsilon (t)\leq C\, t^{-1/(m-2)},\qquad \max _{N_ t}|A|=O(t^{1/(m-2)}).  \] Rescaling about the intersection point by $\varepsilon (t)^{-1}$ gives the Lawlor neck locally smoothly, and the curvature becomes unbounded. These are asymptotic estimates from a parabolic gluing construction, not an exact formula for $N_ t$. The singular limiting union does not make the regular slices nonembedded. No symmetry, uniqueness, or uniform mean-curvature decay is asserted. Euclidean Gaussian quantities are not assigned in this torus ambient space. text: These are surface flows of codimension two in a hyperkahler four-manifold. DE8829990703 (Infinite-time curvature blow-up with vanishing mean curvature) Use the Gibbons–Hawking setting of [ LeeTsai2026 ] , Section 2: the circle quotient contains the collinear centers $(a_ j,0,0)$ with $-1=a_1<\cdots <a_ N=1$, $N\geq 3$, and \[  \varphi =\varphi _{\rm reg}+\frac12\sum _{j=1}^ N ((x-a_ j)^2+y^2+z^2)^{-1/2},\qquad g=\varphi ^{-1}\eta ^2+\varphi (dx^2+dy^2+dz^2), \quad d\eta =*d\varphi .  \] The regular part is smooth, nonnegative, and harmonic on the source's quotient neighborhood. Let the initial Lagrangian sphere be the smooth circle lift of a positive concave graph $(x,u_0(x),0)$ joining the outer centers, with $u_0(\pm 1)=0$. For fixed $\Lambda >0$, require the small-slope and curvature conditions of Theorem 6.2: \[  |u_0'|\leq c^{-1},\qquad -u_0''\leq \Lambda u_0\varphi (x,u_0,0),  \] where $c$ is sufficiently large as supplied by that theorem. Theorem 6.2 proves \[  \sup |\vec H|\longrightarrow 0,\qquad 0<\liminf _{t\to \infty }\frac{\log \max |A|}{\sqrt t} \leq \limsup _{t\to \infty }\frac{\log \max |A|}{\sqrt t}<\infty .  \] Finite-time slices have genus zero, no ends, and are complete and proper. text: 3CC118326D79 (Cohomogeneity-two special Lagrangians) Let $m\geq 3$, $d=m-1$, $I=(-\pi /(2d),\pi /(2d))$, $\mu _1,\mu _2>0$, and $\varphi \in \mathbb R$. Define \[  r(s)=(\cos (ds))^{-1/d},\quad \ell (s)=r(s)e^{is},\quad B(s)=\int _0^ s r(v)^2\, dv.  \] For $u\in S^{m-2}\subset \mathbb R^{m-1}$ and $(x,y)\in I^2$, put \[  X(u,x,y)=\left(e^{i\varphi }\mu _1\mu _2\ell (x)\ell (y)u, \frac{\mu _2^2r(y)^2-\mu _1^2r(x)^2}{2} +i\bigl (\mu _2^2B(y)-\mu _1^2B(x)\bigr )\right)\in \mathbb C^ m.  \] This is an exact integral parametrization of an embedded, exact special Lagrangian of dimension and codimension $m$. Thus $\vec H=0$ and $L_ t=X(S^{m-2}\times I^2)$ for every $t\in \mathbb R$. It is the $G=SO(m-1)$ case of [ SuWood2026 ] , equation (31), Theorem 5.6, Proposition 5.9 and Remark 5.10. It has cohomogeneity two under this group; for $m=3$ the topology is $S^1\times \mathbb R^2$, not a surface annulus. The topology in general is $S^{m-2}\times \mathbb R^2$, with one end. The parametrization is proper: approaching either endpoint of $I$ makes $|\ell (x)\ell (y)|$ diverge, and the remaining factor $u$ is compact. The induced metric is therefore complete. The calibrated image is stable under compactly supported variations. No entropy value or global asymptotic classification is recorded here. title: 5.38 Stolarski–Su finite-time Lagrangian neck pinches
text: 41748F7ED1C1 (Prescribed Type II blow-up rates) For $n\geq 4$ and every integer $K\geq 2$, and for $n=3$ with $K\in \{ 2,3,4\} $, [ StolarskiSu2026 ] , Theorem 1.1 and Remark 1, construct smooth noncompact properly embedded exact almost-calibrated Lagrangian mean curvature flows $L(t)\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $0\leq t<T<\infty $. Here we record the $SO(n)$-invariant subfamily, of dimension and codimension $n$. Its topology is $S^{n-1}\times \mathbb R$, with two ends, and every regular slice is complete. The topology follows from the global profile graph and its spherical group orbits. The origin is a finite-time Type II singularity with \[  0<\liminf _{t\uparrow T}(T-t)^{K/2}\sup _{L(t)}|A| \leq \limsup _{t\uparrow T}(T-t)^{K/2}\sup _{L(t)}|A|<\infty .  \] The unique tangent flow is a stationary multiplicity-one pair of transverse special Lagrangian planes. In contrast, the finer rescaling satisfies \[  (T-t)^{-K/2}L(t)\longrightarrow aL \quad \hbox{smoothly on compact sets},\qquad a>0,  \] where $L$ is the rotational Lawlor neck. Up to a fixed unitary rotation, that limiting neck has the exact parametrization \[  X(u,\theta )=(\sin (n\theta ))^{-1/n}e^{i\theta }u, \quad u\in S^{n-1},\quad 0<\theta <\pi /n.  \] This is a formula for the blow-up limit, not for $L(t)$. The actual flow is constructed by solving a nonlinear parabolic problem near a modulated neck of scale comparable to $(T-t)^{K/2}$, and has no closed formula. The initial Lagrangian angle oscillation can be arbitrarily small. These existence and convergence statements do not assert dynamical stability, uniqueness of the initial data, or a numerical entropy value. The illustration uses the exact Lawlor profile above with a prescribed scale to show the near-singularity dynamics. With a reference time $t_0<T$, write \[  \tau =\frac{t-t_0}{T-t_0},\qquad q=1-\tau ,\qquad a_{\mathrm{model}}(\tau )=a_0q^{K/2}.  \] Here $a_0$ and the equality defining $a_{\mathrm{model}}$ are choices for the drawing, not an exact formula for the modulation parameter of the flow. section: 5.30 Ancient dense torus curves with irrational frequencies
text: 3E693532AA77 Choose $m\geq 2$, amplitudes $a_ j>0$, and positive frequencies $\omega _ j$ which are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$. For $\theta ,\tau \in \mathbb R$, set \[  C(\theta ,\tau )=\bigl (a_ j e^{-\omega _ j^2\tau }\cos (\omega _ j\theta ), a_ j e^{-\omega _ j^2\tau }\sin (\omega _ j\theta )\bigr )_{j=1}^ m, \qquad t(\tau )=-\frac12\sum _{j=1}^ m a_ j^2e^{-2\omega _ j^2\tau }.  \] The strictly increasing map $\tau \mapsto t$ maps $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty ,0)$. These formulas therefore define an ancient curve-shortening flow in $\mathbb R^{2m}$, of dimension one and codimension $2m-1$. They are explicit in the auxiliary time $\tau $; physical time generally requires inversion of the displayed scalar relation. Indeed, with \[  D(\tau )=\sum _ j\omega _ j^2a_ j^2e^{-2\omega _ j^2\tau }, \qquad \frac{dt}{d\tau }=D,  \] one has $|C_\theta |^2=D$, $C_\tau =C_{\theta \theta }$, and $C_ t=C_{ss}$. This direct differentiation fixes the coefficient in the time relation. At each finite time the curve is an injective immersion of $\mathbb R$, dense in the product of the $m$ coordinate circles. It is not an embedding: recurrence gives sequences escaping in the parameter whose images converge to a point of the curve. It is also not proper. Its constant positive speed makes its induced metric complete. Its parameter manifold is noncompact with two intrinsic ends, although its image is bounded and neither end escapes every compact set. The closure is a torus; the evolving object is a curve, not that torus as a surface. The flow has simultaneous rotational symmetry and is not homothetically self-similar because distinct coordinate radii have changing ratios. The exact radius and curvature identities are \[  |C|^2=-2t,\qquad |C_{ss}|^2=\frac{\sum _ j\omega _ j^4 a_ j^2e^{-2\omega _ j^2\tau }}{D(\tau )^2}.  \] Thus curvature is constant along each time slice. After dividing by $\sqrt{-2t}$, the largest-frequency coordinate pair dominates as $t\to -\infty $, and the smallest-frequency pair dominates as $t\uparrow 0$. The locally parametrized limits are great circles traced by an unbounded parameter; no finite-multiplicity convergence is asserted for the full recurrent curve. At a fixed time, the infinite length lies in a bounded set. Consequently every positive-scale Gaussian length integral is infinite, and both $F_{0,1}$ and entropy are $+\infty $. This is a direct consequence of the parametrization, with length counted on the immersed domain. No finite Gaussian-area or locally finite length assertion is intended. For the illustrated $\mathbb R^4$ case take $a_1=a_2=1$ and $(\omega _1,\omega _2)=(1,\sqrt2)$. An explicit physical-time formula is obtained by setting \[  u(t)=\frac{\sqrt{1-8t}-1}{2},\qquad C(\theta ,t)=\bigl (\sqrt u\cos \theta ,\sqrt u\sin \theta , u\cos (\sqrt2\theta ),u\sin (\sqrt2\theta )\bigr ),\qquad t<0.  \] Source: [ AAAW13 ] , Section 3, equations (11)–(14), PDF pp. 8–10. The irrational-frequency case is distinct from the compact rational-frequency family in 5.29 . The figure samples a finite parameter interval and projects four-dimensional geometry; apparent crossings in this projection do not establish self-intersections in $\mathbb R^4$. text: 4973C84D3B2B The nonclosed branch of the planar shrinking-curve classification is recorded in [ Halldorsson2012 ] , Theorem 5.1 and Section 5, PDF pp. 11–13. These are smooth complete immersed curves $X:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R^2$ of codimension one, in the normalization $\vec H=-X^\perp /2$. With arclength $s$, left normal $N=iT$, and signed curvature $k$, solve \[  u'=uv,\qquad v'=\frac12-u^2,\qquad \theta '=u,\qquad X(s)=-2i e^{i\theta (s)}(u(s)+iv(s)).  \] Here $u(0)=r_{\min }/2$, $v(0)=0$, $\theta (0)=0$ and $0<r_{\min }<\sqrt2$. The phase orbit $(u,v)$ is periodic; write $P$ for its period and $\alpha =(2\pi )^{-1}\int _0^ P u(s)\, ds$. Choose $r_{\min }$ so that $\alpha $ is irrational. The period analysis gives $1/2<\alpha <1/\sqrt2$, and every irrational value in this interval occurs. This is an ODE construction with an irrational turning condition, not a closed formula. The image is dense in the annulus $r_{\min }\leq |X|\leq r_{\max }$, where \[  r_{\min }e^{-r_{\min }^2/4}=r_{\max }e^{-r_{\max }^2/4}, \qquad r_{\max }>\sqrt2.  \] Successive radial excursions are congruent by rotation through $2\pi \alpha $. The curvature is positive and periodic, with $k e^{-|X|^2/4}$ constant: local strict convexity does not imply global embeddedness. The curve is nonembedded and nonproper. Its parameter manifold is the noncompact line, with two intrinsic ends, despite its bounded image; neither end escapes to spatial infinity. Completeness follows from the global unit-speed parametrization. The annulus is the image closure, not a two-dimensional flow. The exact evolution from this ODE-defined profile is $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, X(\mathbb R)$, $-\infty <t<0$, interpreted as a parametrized immersion. At every regular time its Gaussian area and entropy are infinite, with arclength counted on the parameter domain: an infinite-length curve lies in a bounded set, so every fixed Gaussian weight is bounded below there. This elementary consequence is separate from the source classification. No finite-entropy or stability theorem is claimed for this branch. For rational $\alpha =m/\ell $, the curve closes and is already recorded in Example 2.1 ; the circle and stationary line are Examples 2.9 and 2.10 . One complete excursion is highlighted, and its rotated continuations show how the image approaches density as the displayed parameter window grows. At time $t<0$, the annular radii are $\sqrt{-t}\, r_{\min }$ and $\sqrt{-t}\, r_{\max }$. The dashed circles are guides to the image closure, not additional components. The limit $t=0$ is not a regular immersed time slice. E9086532F53A Section 5 of [ Halldorsson2013 ] , PDF pp. 12–14, derives the classical helicoidal minimal surfaces and attributes them to Wunderlich. For $h>0$, $a\in \mathbb R$, and $(u,\phi )\in \mathbb R^2$, an exact formula is \[  X(u)=(h\sinh (hu)+ia\cosh (hu))e^{-iau},\qquad F(u,\phi )=(e^{i\phi }X(u),h\phi ).  \] A constant horizontal rotation may be included. The profile parameter $u$ is not arclength; in the notation of the source, $	au =h\sinh (hu)$ and $s=(a^2+h^2)	au /h^2$. These codimension-one minimal immersions in $\mathbb R^3$ give exact eternal stationary flows $M_ t=F(\mathbb R^2)$ for all $t\in \mathbb R$. For $a=0$, changing variable $r=h\sinh (hu)$ gives the usual embedded helicoid $(r\cos \phi ,r\sin \phi ,h\phi )$, $r,\phi \in \mathbb R$. For $a
e 0$, the profile has infinitely many self-intersections, which give self-intersections of the surface at the same height. In each case the parameter manifold is a complete proper noncompact plane, of genus zero and one end. Properness follows directly from $|X(u)|	o \infty $ and $F_3=h\phi $; completeness also follows from properness of the immersion. The screw symmetry has pitch $h$, with vertical period $2\pi h$ as a symmetry of the image. Genus and ends here describe the full parameter plane, not a quotient by that vertical period. For $a
e 0$, the profile has minimum radius $|a|$, reflection symmetry, constant-sign curvature tending to zero on both arms, and $rT/X	o \pm (h-ia)/\sqrt{h^2+a^2}$. These are properties of the generating curve, not convexity of the minimal surface. For fixed $a
e 0$, its arclength parametrization tends locally smoothly to the circle $ia e^{-is/a}$ as $h	o 0$. Another scaling gives the limiting profile \[  X_0(s)= rac{s^{1-ib}}{1-ib},\qquad s>0,\quad b\in \mathbb R, \qquad s^{1-ib}=s e^{-ib\log s}.  \] This logarithmic spiral is a limiting generating curve in equation (5.4), not itself a claimed planar curve-shortening soliton; the zero-pitch surface parametrization is degenerate. No entropy, Gaussian-area or stability classification is recorded here. Section 6 studies helicoidal surfaces of nonzero constant mean curvature for comparison. Constant mean curvature alone does not make them stationary or self-similar solutions of ordinary MCF, so that comparison family is not added as a new special flow. Its round cylindrical case is already represented by Example 2.19 . The figures sample the exact formula, with parameters $h$ and $a$ and interactive rotation and zoom. title: 2.25 Drugan–Kleene immersed shrinking families
text: C28E16016422 For every $n\geq 2$, Drugan–Kleene construct infinitely many complete rotational immersed self-shrinkers in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ of each topology $S^ n$, $\mathbb R^ n$, $\mathbb R\times S^{n-1}$ and $S^1\times S^{n-1}$. This expands the single sphere construction in Example 2.24 ; it does not identify the torus examples with Angenent's embedded torus. The arclength meridian $(x,r)$ satisfies \[  x'=\cos \alpha ,\quad r'=\sin \alpha ,\quad \alpha '=\frac{x}{2}\sin \alpha +\left(\frac{n-1}{r}-\frac r2\right)\cos \alpha .  \] A smooth axis endpoint must meet the axis orthogonally. Closed meridians generate tori; the other endpoint conditions distinguish spheres, planes and cylinders. The existence proof uses shooting and limiting geodesics; arbitrary initial data do not produce one of these complete examples. The flow is $M_ t=\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $, $-\infty <t<0$. Nontrivial rotational spheres, planes and cylinders in this construction are not embedded, by the rotational classification quoted in the source. No blanket embedding or uniqueness assertion is made for the torus branch. Sources: [ DruganKleene2017 ] . title: 2.51 Riedler shrinkers from isoparametric foliations
text: 395E0B7648CA Let $M^{n-1}\subset S^ n$ be a closed isoparametric hypersurface with equal principal-curvature multiplicities. Riedler constructs a closed embedded shrinking hypersurface of topology $S^1\times M$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, formed from homothetic copies of leaves of the associated isoparametric foliation. In this entry we retain the cases with $g=3,4,6$ distinct principal curvatures. The $g=1$ case is Angenent's torus; the $g=2$ product-of-spheres case is deliberately omitted from this addition. For equal multiplicity $m$, $n-1=gm$. One example is $S^1\times SO(3)/(\mathbb Z_2\times \mathbb Z_2)\subset \mathbb R^5$. The admissible multiplicities are those of an existing spherical isoparametric foliation; arbitrary $(g,m)$ are not allowed. A shooting argument closes a geodesic in the two-dimensional orbit metric. This is an ODE existence construction, not an elementary parametrization. The resulting hypersurface is compact, complete and proper, and its flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$. No uniqueness or stability statement is asserted here. For an arclength curve $\gamma :I\to \mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $, the map \[  F(s,p)=\gamma (s)\psi (p)  \] is Lagrangian in $\mathbb C^ n$. It satisfies $\mathbf H+\lambda F^\perp =0$ precisely when \[  k=\langle \gamma ,N\rangle \left(\frac{n-1}{|\gamma |^2}-\lambda \right).  \] Writing $\gamma =re^{i\phi }$ and $\alpha $ for tangent angle minus $\phi $, the profile equations are $r'=\cos \alpha $, $\phi '=\sin \alpha /r$, $\alpha '=(\lambda r-n/r)\sin \alpha $. title: 3.20 Convex slab translators with polyhedral asymptotics
search_title: Convex slab translators with polyhedral asymptotics
section: 3.20 Convex slab translators with polyhedral asymptotics
text: F05CE3FF1C12 Bourni–Langford–Tinaglia construct convex slab translators from an unbounded regular circumscribed polytope $P\subset \mathbb R^ n$ that does not split a line, and separately from circumscribed unbounded simplices. Here circumscribed means that the defining facets are tangent to the unit sphere with the orientations in the source; regularity is the source's symmetry condition on the polytope, not arbitrary polyhedral data. The resulting hypersurface lies in $(-\pi /2,\pi /2)\times \mathbb R^ n$, lies in no smaller slab, and its translating evolution sweeps out that slab. Its blow-down under the linear ancient-time scale (the source's “squash-down”) is $P$. The regular construction is locally uniformly convex, reflection symmetric in the slab midplane, and inherits the symmetries of $P$. The evolution is an exact translation of the constructed hypersurface for all real times; the speed and direction are determined by the polyhedral data. There is no closed height formula or general uniqueness claim here. The diagram illustrates a higher-dimensional polyhedral section, not the curvature or topology of a surface in $\mathbb R^3$. Lower-dimensional overlapping slab examples are cross-referenced to Example 3.9 . Sources: [ BourniLangfordTinaglia2022 ] . title: 3.19 Castro–Lerma Lagrangian translators from curve pairs

section: 3.19 Castro–Lerma Lagrangian translators from curve pairs
text: B4DA2A79EC96 Castro–Lerma construct Lagrangian translating immersions in $\mathbb C^2$ from pairs of planar soliton curves. In the shrinker–expander case, choose nonvanishing arclength curves $\alpha (s),\omega (u)$ with curvature vectors $\mathbf k_\alpha =-\alpha ^\perp $ and $\mathbf k_\omega =\omega ^\perp $. Their product construction has the integral form \[  F(s,u)=\left(\int ^ u\omega '(v)\overline{\omega (v)}\, dv- \int ^ s\alpha '(v)\overline{\alpha (v)}\, dv,\; \alpha (s)\omega (u)\right).  \] The translator velocity in this normalization is $(1,0)\in \mathbb C^2$. The induced metric is $(|\alpha |^2+|\omega |^2)(ds^2+du^2)$, so complete profile parameters bounded away from simultaneous zero give complete immersions. The more general rotating/dilating curve pairs are treated in Proposition 2; they are not all asserted to be embedded or proper. The flow is $F+t(1,0)$ for $t\in \mathbb R$. Choosing a circular shrinker and a nonstraight expander provides a concrete numerical example. The already listed Hamiltonian-stationary translator and Joyce–Lee–Tsui overlap are not new examples here. The visualized two-dimensional sheet is a projection from four real dimensions, with coordinate choice shown in the controls. Sources: [ CastroLerma2012 ] . title: 3.25 Su–Wood Lagrangian translating helicoids
text: 6386C95CB0EA Use the Su–Wood Ansatz with $a=1$ and an admissible compact group $G\subset SU(m-1)$ acting on $\mathbb C^{m-1}$ with isotropic orbits of dimension $m-2$. If $\gamma ,\xi $ are the regular (with the smooth extension at a line profile's origin understood) profile curves satisfying equation (1) of the source, its profile map is \[  \check F(x,y)=\left(\gamma (x)\xi (y),\;  \int ^ y \xi '(v)\overline{\xi (v)}\, dv- \int ^ x\gamma '(u)\overline{\gamma (u)}\, du\right).  \] The full Lagrangian is the $G$-orbit of the specified linear inclusion of $\check F$ into $\mathbb C^ m$ and translates in $\operatorname {Re}z_ m$. The source uses opposite profile soliton constants for the two factors. It is the induced orbit geometry, not ordinary planar curve shortening, that gives the Anciaux profile equation. Example 1 takes a line and a nonconstant closed Anciaux shrinker profile, with $G=SO(m-1)$. The resulting image is a smooth embedded translating helicoid, periodic in $\operatorname {Im}z_ m$; the nonconstant profile distinguishes it from the already recorded constant-radius rotating translator. For other groups the analogous construction can have a one-dimensional singular set and is not included in this smooth case. The associated motion is translation for every real time. The plotted object is the two-dimensional profile projection used in Figures 1–2, not the full $m$-dimensional Lagrangian. The source explicitly does not claim new complete smooth embedded almost-calibrated translators from this Ansatz. title: 3.27 Nonconvex entire graphical translators
text: 879611BCBD19 The 2026 preprint of Dávila–del Pino–Wei states that for every $N\ge 8$ there is a one-parameter family of entire smooth functions $G:\mathbb R^ N\to \mathbb R$ satisfying \[  \operatorname {div}\frac{DG}{\sqrt{1+|DG|^2}}=\frac1{\sqrt{1+|DG|^2}},  \] whose graphs are not convex. The graphs are embedded, complete and proper, with topology $\mathbb R^ N$, and translate with unit vertical velocity for $t\in \mathbb R$. The positive scalar quantity in the displayed graph equation expresses mean convexity with the source's normal convention; it does not imply nonnegative principal curvatures. The construction in $N=8$ perturbs Bombieri–De Giorgi–Giusti geometry; higher dimensions follow by flat products. It is separate from the convex Wang examples. This is a reported preprint construction, with no independent proof verification or stability conclusion recorded here. Its profile is not available as a closed formula. The figure is a labeled radial-coordinate schematic of the two four-dimensional blocks and the transition near the Simons cone; the plotted saddle is not an exact translator or a surface MCF in three-space. section: 4.4 Graphical expanders from general Lipschitz cones
text: 9A84A12D805C Let $u_0:\mathbb R^ n\to \mathbb R$ be globally Lipschitz and positively homogeneous of degree one. The unique graphical mean curvature flow from this cone is smooth for $t>0$ and respects parabolic scaling. Thus \[  u(x,t)=\sqrt t\, U(x/\sqrt t),\qquad \left(\delta _{ij}-\frac{U_ iU_ j}{1+|DU|^2}\right)U_{ij} =\frac{U-x\cdot DU}{2}.  \] The graph of $U$ is a complete proper embedded hypersurface diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ n$. For cones smooth away from the vertex, the asymptotic statement is understood away from that vertex. This graphical construction does not require rotational symmetry or mean convexity; its uniqueness is in the corresponding graphical evolution class. A concrete nonsymmetric cone for illustration is $u_0(r,\theta )=0.35r\cos (2\theta )$ in $\mathbb R^3$. It is globally Lipschitz and is not the round cone of the existing rotational entry. The displayed positive-time surfaces are finite-domain numerical graphical MCF approximations; the truncation boundary and refinement error are separate from the complete existence theorem. title: 4.19 Expanders based on generalized Lawson–Osserman maps

section: 4.19 Expanders based on generalized Lawson–Osserman maps
text: 42620E4B40CF Let $L:S^ n\to S^ m$ be a Lawson–Osserman map with equal nonzero singular values (LOMSE) of admissible type $(n,p,k)$. Assume $(n,p,k)=(3,2,2),(5,4,2),(5,4,4)$, or $n\ge 7$. Chen-Kuan Lee constructs, for sufficiently small positive prescribed data $f(R)=\varepsilon R$, a smooth self-expander \[  F(r,x)=(rx,f(r)L(x))\in \mathbb R^{n+m+2},\quad r\ge 0,\  x\in S^ n.  \] It is an entire graph over $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, hence embedded, complete and proper, with one end. The radial function satisfies $f=O(r^ k)$, $f'=O(r^{k-1})$ at zero, $f,f'\ge 0$, and $f(r)/r\to \varphi _\infty $ at infinity. The limiting cone has slope $\varphi _\infty $; it is not automatically the minimal Lawson–Osserman cone. Uniqueness additionally requires $0\le f\le \varepsilon r$ and $0\le f'\le (2k-1)f/r$ on $(0,R]$. The Hopf map $S^3\to S^2$ gives the first case: a four-dimensional graph in $\mathbb R^7$. The source uses $\mathbf H=F^\perp $; dilation by $\sqrt2$ converts the profile to $\mathbf H=F^\perp /2$, whose flow is $\sqrt t\, \Sigma $, $t>0$. The figure shows radial data, not a seven-dimensional embedding in three-space. title: 5.1 The ancient sine wave
text: 3BF94583DFB1 An exact eternal graphical solution of planar curve shortening is \[  X(x,t)=(x,\operatorname {arsinh}(e^{-t}\sin x)),\qquad x\in \mathbb R,\quad t\in \mathbb R.  \] Writing its height as $u$, direct differentiation gives $u_ t=u_{xx}/(1+u_ x^2)$; this also fixes the time normalization. Spatial translations, time translations and parabolic dilations give the usual equivalent versions. Nakayama–Iizuka–Wadati's ancient sine wave is recalled in Angenent–You's introduction. Each slice is complete, proper and embedded, with parameter topology $\mathbb R$, two ends and period $2\pi $ in $x$. It is nonconvex and has infinite total absolute curvature, because each spatial period has a positive curvature integral. At each fixed finite time its slope is bounded, so it has finite Gaussian area and entropy, without a uniform-in-time value asserted here. section: 5.8 Immersed ancient curves spanning a half-plane
text: 4B3B50761BB9 Ma constructs a compact immersed ancient curve-shortening flow in $\mathbb R^2$ whose time-slice convex hulls together fill a half-plane. Compactness refers to each individual immersed closed curve, not to a uniform spatial bound over ancient time. The construction joins increasingly complicated grim-reaper configurations and takes an ancient limit; it is not a homothetic curve or an explicit parametrization. The curves can have crossings at early times and become embedded later, then shrink to a round point. Hence embeddedness is time dependent. Smooth compact slices are complete and proper as immersions, have no ends, and have finite Gaussian area and entropy at each time; no uniform ancient-time bound is claimed. The source's sequence of disappearing fingers is a guide to the construction, not a formula for singular events of the final ancient limit. Our diagram separates early immersed stages from the later embedded stage and labels them as qualitative stages rather than numerically computed MCF slices. text: 1A07DD8D8A69 Bourni–Mramor construct a nonplanar eternal curve-shortening flow in $\mathbb R^3$ by joining grim-reaper pieces in distinct planes. The complete embedded slices are ramps: a fixed directional component of the unit tangent has a controlled sign, a property used to prevent singularities and continue the ancient limit forward. title: 5.19 Rotational collapsed ancient pancakes
text: 325F4A3220BC For each $n\ge 2$, Bourni–Langford–Tinaglia construct a compact strictly convex ancient hypersurface in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ invariant under $O(1)\times O(n)$, contained in a slab of width $\pi $ and in no smaller slab. The smooth flow exists for $t<0$ and becomes extinct at the origin at $t=0$, after normalization. Each slice has topology $S^ n$ and is embedded, complete and proper. Backward in time, the two large faces approach the boundary hyperplanes of the slab, while appropriately translated edge regions approach grim hyperplanes. These are collapsed ancient solutions, distinct from the noncollapsed ancient ovals and from nonconvex stacked pancakes. The source constructs them by flowing rotated Angenent ovals and passing to a limit. Rotating a planar Angenent oval is not itself an exact higher-dimensional ancient solution. The picture therefore labels its rounded pancake profiles as schematics and marks the fixed slab walls and grim edge regions; it does not claim to compute the ancient limit. Compactness gives finite entropy at every fixed time, with no value asserted here. title: 5.33 Ancient ovals with reduced symmetry
text: F18DC5F92665 For $n\ge 3$ and $2\le k\le n-1$, Du–Haslhofer construct $(k-1)$-parameter families of compact ancient noncollapsed mean-convex hypersurfaces in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ with $\mathbb Z_2^ k\times O(n+1-k)$ symmetry. title: 5.22 Non-self-similar ancient doughnuts
text: 7A6AD2F58C6E For each $n\ge 2$, Bourni–Langford–Mramor construct a closed embedded rotational ancient flow with topology $S^1\times S^{n-1}$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ that is not a soliton. It is obtained by perturbing a shrinking doughnut inward and taking an ancient limit. In rescaled coordinates the backward limit is a shrinking doughnut; the finite-time evolution is not a family of homothetic copies of that limit. The source explains that the flow develops a circle of neck-pinch singularities at the forward endpoint. The regular slices are compact, complete and proper. section: 5.32 Ancient isoparametric flows in Euclidean space
text: 199B3435F93B Liu–Terng prove that the spherical and Euclidean mean curvature flows starting at a compact isoparametric submanifold $M^ n\subset S^{n+k-1}$ extend for all backward time. Isoparametric means flat normal bundle and constant principal curvatures along parallel normal fields. The nonminimal leaves give nonstationary spherical flows and nonhomothetic Euclidean flows. They approach the unique parallel minimal isoparametric leaf backward in the respective normalization, and collapse forward to a focal submanifold. If $f(s,\cdot )$ is the spherical flow, the Euclidean flow is \[  F(t,\cdot )=\sqrt{1-2nt}\, f\left(-\frac{\log (1-2nt)}{2n},\cdot \right).  \] A concrete exact case is the product $S^ p(\sqrt{A-2pt})\times S^ q(\sqrt{B-2qt})\subset \mathbb R^{p+q+2}$, for $t<\min (A/(2p),B/(2q))$, with $A/p\ne B/q$. This gives a nonhomothetic ancient flow; the equal-extinction case is already a spherical shrinker. The $(p,q)=(1,1)$ figure projects the exact product tori from four-space, retaining both radii separately. Smooth compact slices are embedded, complete and proper, and their topology remains that of the initial regular leaf before the focal event. The general isoparametric families also include flag-manifold examples. The explicit product picture illustrates one case, not all such leaves. Here each orbit has dimension $n-1$ and the same isotropy type. Madnick–Wood construct an almost-calibrated Lagrangian MCF developing a Type II singularity at the origin for which every Type II blow-up is $L_\infty $ and every Type I blow-up is its asymptotic cone. The profile flow in a complex line is \[  (\partial _ t\gamma )^\perp =\mathbf k-(n-1)\frac{\gamma ^\perp }{|\gamma |^2}.  \] It is not ordinary planar curve shortening. Admissible non-$SO(n)$ groups, for example the diagonal $T^{n-1}$ action, give models beyond the currently listed rotational Lawlor neck. The theorem concerns the evolving singularity-forming flow; its stationary special Lagrangian limit is not counted as an additional moving soliton. Smoothness is restricted to the source's constant-isotropy stratum. We do not infer full embeddedness or topology solely from a projected profile. The illustration uses an exact model profile with a schematic neck scale, clearly distinguished from the nonlinear flow constructed in the proof.
