title: 2.29 Lens-shaped shrinking surface clusters
text: 521D2D744A5F Baldi–Haus–Mantegazza construct a rotationally symmetric self-shrinking lens-shaped cluster in $\mathbb R^3$. Two bounded disk-type caps and an unbounded planar exterior meet along a common circle at $120$ degrees. The upper and lower caps are exchanged by reflection in the horizontal plane. Each sheet satisfies $\mathbf H=-X^\perp /2$ away from the triple circle; the equal-angle condition supplies the junction balance. The flow is homothetic for $t<0$. This is a cluster with a junction curve, not a smooth closed sphere or an immersed surface without boundary. The exterior sheet gives a noncompact cluster; the caps themselves are compact disks. Surface genus for the whole singular union is inapplicable. The source proves existence by shooting a rotational profile; it does not identify the caps with spherical caps. The picture therefore uses a numerical rotational shooting profile and keeps the exterior planar sheet, triple circle and $120$-degree contact distinct. Gaussian integrals use the sum of sheet areas, with no numerical entropy value assigned. title: 2.20 Rotational shrinking trumpet ends
text: 41C51DD59791 For every positive asymptotic slope, Kleene–Møller construct a rotational shrinking trumpet end in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge 2$, asymptotic to the corresponding round cone. In graph coordinates $r=u(x)>0$ the profile solves $u''=(1+u'^2)(xu'/2-u/2+(n-1)/u)$. The theorem concerns an end with an inner boundary; it must not be presented as a complete boundaryless rotational shrinker. The radial cone is an asymptote, not the trumpet itself. Its smooth rotational sheets are embedded on the stated end, and the geometry is noncompact. We display numerical far-field shooting on a finite interval, with the inner boundary and cutoff explicitly marked. Under the normalization $\mathbf H=-X^\perp /2$, the end evolves as $\sqrt{-t}\, \Sigma $ for $t<0$, including motion of its inner boundary. No boundary condition for a separate fixed-barrier MCF problem is imposed. No global entropy or uniqueness conclusion beyond the cited end problem is recorded. section: 4.1 Expanding planar networks with a bounded cell
text: 4D33C840252C In the equal-tension case, Chen–Guo construct a regular self-expanding planar network with one bounded central cell and $k$ exterior rays for every integer $k\ge 7$. Every junction has angle $120$ degrees. The global existence condition in their Theorem 2 is $\sum _ i\psi _{i,i+1}>2\pi $; equal tensions give $\psi _{i,i+1}=\pi /3$, hence exactly $k>6$ for this construction. Six sides belong to the stationary limiting balance and do not give a nontrivial expander of this type. In our normalization the branches satisfy $\mathbf k=X^\perp /2$ and the flow is $\sqrt t\, \Gamma $, $t>0$. This network has a cycle and is not covered by the planar-tree entry. The source proves uniqueness within its prescribed contact-angle and radial-interface ansatz, not among all networks with the same number of ends. The parameter graph is complete and embedded with its prescribed junctions; it has $k$ ends and finite Gaussian area and entropy. Our numerical shooting constructs the symmetric seven-sided example, with radial exterior rays. A changing side count changes the family member; the time slider only applies homothety. title: 4.11 Reported multiphase expanding surface constructions
text: 55F8A309578D Liao's 2025 preprint proposes self-expanding multiphase surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ with regular triple curves and tetrahedral quadruple points, obtained from weighted-area minimization with prescribed asymptotic interface data. Triple sheets meet at $120$ degrees; four triple curves have the tetrahedral angle $\arccos (-1/3)$. The intended flow is $\sqrt t\, \Gamma $, $t>0$, sheetwise away from junctions. This entry records a reported construction, not a verified existence theorem of this catalogue. The compactness, persistence of junctions and conformal comparison used in Sections 3–5 require further checking. In particular one must distinguish the expander-weighted Euclidean metric from the hyperbolic metric; a conformal comparison does not automatically transport minimality or area minimization. Accordingly no definite global topology, embeddedness, completeness, uniqueness, or entropy assertion is assigned here. The tetrahedral junction drawing illustrates the local angle model only; that stationary cone by itself is not a new nontrivial self-expander. The panels are explicitly labeled proposed smoothing stages, rather than computed or proved flow slices. The backward limit is an equatorial disk; forward the solution contracts to a point on the boundary sphere. The uniqueness statements of Bourni–Langford are within the convex ancient classes and normalizations of their theorems, not for all free-boundary ancient flows. The slices are compact embedded disks, smooth up to their moving boundary. Their boundary is constrained to the unit sphere, unlike a freely shrinking boundary under homothety. The maximal interval is ancient with a finite forward endpoint. For $n=1$ the topology is an interval; for $n=2$ it is a disk of genus zero. These are manifolds with boundary, so completeness means completeness as compact metric spaces, not geodesic completeness without boundary. text: 9FAA74B5E7DA Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^2$ be a smooth bounded strictly convex domain, and let $D$ be an orthogonal diameter: a straight segment in $\overline\Omega $ meeting $\partial \Omega $ orthogonally at both endpoints. Bourni–Burns–Catron construct convex ancient free-boundary curve-shortening solutions approaching $D$ backward, one on each side, with the uniqueness qualifications in Theorem 1.1. The unit-disk family is a special case, cross-linked separately. Each regular slice is an embedded compact arc with endpoints moving on the fixed boundary and perpendicular contact there. Its topology is an interval, and it has no noncompact ends. The domain is not scaled with the curve. The construction is by parabolic limits, not an explicit family of elliptical arcs. text: FB8BC9B105B9 In the unit disk fix $o=(-d,0)$, with $0<d\le 1$. Langford–Liu–McNamara construct ancient curve-shortening flows with one endpoint fixed at $o$ (Dirichlet condition) and the other moving on the unit circle with orthogonal contact (Neumann condition). For $0<d<1$, the distinguished flow is eternal and connects the longer unstable stationary segment backward to the shorter stable stationary segment forward. At $d=1$ the forward endpoint is a finite-time singularity with a half-grim-reaper Type II model. The regular curves are embedded compact intervals. Their endpoints obey different conditions, so the construction is neither the two-free-endpoint ball flow nor a homothetic shrinker. text: 3846578EAD16 Let $M^{m+1}$ be a compact Riemannian manifold with strictly convex boundary, and let $\Sigma ^ m\subset M$ be a smooth properly embedded two-sided free-boundary minimal hypersurface of Morse index $I>0$. Bourni–Franz's 2026 preprint constructs an $I$-parameter family of ancient free-boundary mean curvature flows backward converging to $\Sigma $. The construction uses adapted normal graphs that preserve the nonlinear orthogonality condition; merely adding an eigenfunction to the position vector is not an exact free-boundary deformation. The uniqueness theorem additionally imposes the specified small graph and decay conditions; its generality must not be inferred solely from the index count. A mean-convex ancient branch is obtained from the first eigenfunction, with further uniqueness under nondegeneracy. Smooth graphical slices preserve the topology and embeddedness of $\Sigma $ and meet the fixed ambient boundary orthogonally. The figure shows a critical-catenoid-type free-boundary background and a schematic unstable displacement, not a computed ancient flow. The preprint's existence and classification are attributed results, with no formal proof verification recorded. section: 2.52 Yamamoto Lagrangian shrinkers in Calabi–Yau cones
text: E540F08E41B0 For every integer $g\ge 1$, Yamamoto constructs a real six-dimensional toric Calabi–Yau cone $C(S)=M_ g$ and a compact Lagrangian shrinking immersion with parameter manifold $\Sigma _ g\times S^1$, where $\Sigma _ g$ is a closed orientable surface of genus $g$. The submanifold has real dimension three and codimension three. This is not a genus-$g$ surface in Euclidean three-space, nor a construction in the flat space $\mathbb C^3$. The construction uses the real form, moment-map level sets and torus action of the chosen toric cone, followed by the radial/phase ODE in Theorem 7.1. For the cone metric $dr^2+r^2g_ S$, write $D_ a(s,r)=(s,ar)$ and $R=r\partial _ r$. After normalizing $\mathbf H=-R^\perp /2$, the flow is $D_{\sqrt{-t}}(L)$ for $t<0$. Compactness of the parameter manifold gives completeness and properness of the immersion; a general embedding assertion is not recorded. The cone vertex is outside the smooth ambient manifold and is approached only at the singular endpoint. The figure is a radial and topology diagram, not a Euclidean isometric rendering of the Calabi–Yau metric. Sources: [ Yamamoto2012 ] . text: 86412C87CEBE In $\mathbb H^2\times \mathbb R$, with $g=dr^2+\sinh ^2r\, d\varphi ^2+dz^2$, Bueno constructs an entire rotational bowl and a one-parameter family of properly embedded translating catenoids. The bowl is a complete disk; each catenoid is a complete annulus with two graphical ends outside a compact set, parametrized by its positive neck radius. These are intrinsic product-metric examples, not the Euclidean bowl and winglike solitons. The source uses the average of the two principal curvatures. Its unit-speed profile satisfies \[  r'=\cos \theta ,\quad z'=\sin \theta ,\quad \theta '=2\cos \theta -\coth (r)\sin \theta .  \] Consequently, with the trace mean-curvature vector used by this catalogue, the same surface evolves by $z\mapsto z+2t$, for every $t\in \mathbb R$. Uniqueness is within the rotational class and the additional asymptotic hypotheses of the source. Numerical meridians are revolved and displayed in the Poincaré-disk product coordinates $\rho =\tanh (r/2)$; Euclidean-looking distances in this drawing are not intrinsic distances. text: 38A33FD9E29C Bueno–López classify translation-invariant translating surfaces in $\mathbb H^2\times \mathbb R$. text: 32D1DDDBF12B For each pitch $h>0$, de Lima–Ramos–dos Santos construct a one-parameter family of complete helicoidal solitons in $\mathbb H^2\times \mathbb R$. In the hyperboloid model a profile $\sigma (u)=(\alpha (u),\sqrt{1+|\alpha (u)|^2})$ generates \[  X(u,v)=(e^{vJ}\alpha (u),\sqrt{1+|\alpha (u)|^2},hv),\qquad u,v\in \mathbb R,  \] where $J(x,y)=(-y,x)$. The profile is determined by the curvature ODE in Section 2, not by an Archimedean spiral. Its trace has two unbounded properly embedded arms spiraling around the center; this does not by itself establish embeddedness of their union or of the full immersion. The surface is a rotator exactly when it is a translator for $-h\partial _ z$ in the source convention. Rotation and vertical translation describe the same evolving sets because of the helicoidal symmetry; they must not be added to double the speed. These are eternal isometric flows. text: 3535C925421E López–Munteanu classify invariant translating surfaces in $SL(2,\mathbb R)$ with its standard left-invariant metric. In Iwasawa coordinates $(x,y,\theta )$, $y>0$ and $\theta \in S^1$, the metric is \[  g=\frac{dx^2+dy^2}{4y^2}+\left(d\theta +\frac{dx}{2y}\right)^2.  \] The invariant subgroups are the parabolic, hyperbolic and elliptic factors $N,A,K$. The driving field is selected from the Killing algebra, and is separate from the field tangent to the invariant orbits. The resulting classification contains explicit special cases and ODE-defined families, as well as minimal stationary exceptions. The source's scalar mean curvature is the average of the principal curvatures: a profile satisfying $H=\langle N,X\rangle $ evolves under trace MCF by the isometries generated by $2X$. Complete Killing motion is eternal, but does not make an incomplete profile complete. Global topology, properness and embeddedness must therefore be checked for the chosen subgroup, profile domain and circle identifications; no blanket assertion is recorded here. The visualization is an orbit-space and fiber diagram in the $\mathbb H^2(-4)$ base with its circle fiber. It does not depict the universal cover as identical to $SL(2,\mathbb R)$ or assign Euclidean metric geometry to the coordinate plot. title: 5.41 Isometric curve-shortening solitons in the hyperbolic plane

section: 5.41 Isometric curve-shortening solitons in the hyperbolic plane
text: 39A0C4D2B77A For every nonzero Minkowski vector $\widetilde v\in \mathbb R^{2,1}$, Woolgar–Xie give a two-parameter family of nontrivial curve-shortening solitons in $\mathbb H^2$. Each is complete, unbounded and properly embedded, with parameter domain $\mathbb R$ and two ends. Its motion is the one-parameter group of hyperbolic isometries determined by the corresponding Killing generator; timelike, null and spacelike types correspond to elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic motions. The ends asymptote to horocycles or geodesics under the restrictions in Theorem 1.2. In particular both ends cannot be geodesic-asymptotic, and the timelike case cannot have a geodesic-asymptotic end. The curvature equation is $k_ g=\langle K,N\rangle $; these are eternal isometric flows, not Euclidean shrinkers or homothetically scaled hypercycles. The figure uses a fixed hyperbolic disk or half-plane chart and compares the group motion at three times. Its profile is schematic; no Euclidean curvature conclusion follows from its appearance in the conformal model. Euclidean entropy is inapplicable. text: 4F2C4D7007ED Magaño–Smith prove that there is a generic subset $\mathcal U\subset C^\infty (S^3)$ such that for each $u\in \mathcal U$ there is $\epsilon >0$ with the following property: for every $0<|\delta |<\epsilon $, the fixed metric $g_\delta =e^{2\delta u}g_{\mathrm{round}}$ admits a nontrivial eternal mean curvature flow of embedded tori. The flow parameter ranges over all $t\in \mathbb R$ and is distinct from the small metric parameter $\delta $. The construction perturbs trajectories of the area functional on the space of Clifford tori, using a Morse–Smale argument and a parabolic correction. It is not an explicit radius formula, and the theorem does not assert such a flow in the unperturbed round metric $\delta =0$. Each regular slice is a compact, complete, proper embedded surface of genus one. The figure depicts changing normal graphs over a Clifford-torus background in a labeled projection, with the ambient metric held fixed. The plotted deformations are schematic; they do not compute the generic conformal factor or solve the correction equation. No Euclidean Gaussian area or entropy is assigned. title: 5.42 Finite-time Lagrangian neck pinches with circle symmetry
search_title: Finite-time Lagrangian neck pinches with circle symmetry
section: 5.42 Finite-time Lagrangian neck pinches with circle symmetry
text: A25A9D4CCA2B In an ALE or ALF hyperkähler four-manifold with a tri-Hamiltonian circle action, Lotay–Oliveira analyze the flow of embedded almost-calibrated circle-invariant Lagrangian surfaces. For compact surfaces, or the specified noncompact surfaces asymptotic to a pair of planes, finite-time singularities are neck pinches with the local models established in Theorem 1.1. Their examples guarantee such singularities under the geometric conditions of Section 4. Noncompact examples exist in the nontrivial Gibbons–Hawking settings described there; compact examples require the appropriate configuration of special Lagrangian spheres and phases. This is not a claim for every ambient manifold or every initial Lagrangian. For compact connected initial data, the flow can be continued through finitely many such singular times and converges to an $A_ k$-chain of embedded special Lagrangian spheres, with the precise current and phase conclusions of Theorem 1.4. A single smooth parameter manifold is not retained through a neck pinch. In the Gibbons–Hawking base, the surface is encoded by an arc and circle fibers; the evolution is a weighted curve-shortening equation. The diagram shows the arc approaching a center, the collapsing fiber and the separated chain after the pinch. It is a schematic of the proved mechanism, not a Euclidean surface of revolution asserted to solve the hyperkähler flow. Sources: [ LotayOliveira2023 ] . title: 2.44 Noncompact periodic Lagrangian shrinkers
text: 2DED712E1192 In Joyce–Lee–Tsui, Theorems E–F, choose $1\le m<n$, $\lambda _1=\cdots =\lambda _ m=1$, $\lambda _{m+1}=\cdots =\lambda _ n=-1$, and $C=1$. For the coupled ODE data of Theorems A–B the immersion is \[  L=\{ (x_1w_1(s),\ldots ,x_ nw_ n(s)):\  \sum _ j\lambda _ jx_ j^2=1\} .  \] This entry records the nonconstant-amplitude periodic case. If all phase increments are rational multiples of $\pi $, the $w_ j$ have a common period and the source describes a closed noncompact immersed Lagrangian with parameter topology $S^1\times S^{m-1}\times \mathbb R^{n-m}$. For fixed sign of the soliton parameter such periodic initial data are dense in the allowed data. The $m=1$ parameter quadric has two components, and image identifications must be treated separately. The constant-amplitude Hamiltonian-stationary overlap is already included in the Lee–Wang quadric examples. For negative soliton parameter this is a self-shrinker; after normalization its flow is $\sqrt{-t}\, L$, $t<0$. Periodic bounded nonvanishing amplitudes give completeness and properness of the resulting periodic immersion. The theorem does not assert that every such immersion is embedded. Nonperiodic quasiperiodic data instead give nonclosed images with larger-dimensional closures and are not assigned the same topology or properness. The figure is a phase-loop and indefinite-quadric schematic; it does not falsely replace the coupled ODE by independent sinusoidal phases. title: 3.23 Translators with general closed-shrinker ends
text: 191836516CC9 For a closed smooth embedded self-shrinker $S\subset \mathbb R^ n$ of Gaussian Morse index $I$, Sun–Wang construct an $I$-parameter family of complete embedded translators in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ whose unique tangent flow at backward infinity is $S\times \mathbb R$ with multiplicity one. The construction may have a singular set of dimension at most $n-7$; it is smooth for $n\le 6$, namely ambient dimension at most seven. In higher dimensions it is a weak geometric construction, not an unconditional smooth hypersurface theorem. The Angenent-torus and spherical-doubling input cases have their own existing pages. The topology of a cross-sectional shrinker must not be recorded as the genus of the higher-dimensional translator. The theorem specifies the tangent flow, not a literal product end at finite height. The figure shows increasing asymptotic cross-sections and labels the uncomputed core; no arbitrary tube is asserted to solve the translator equation. title: 5.7 Immersed ancient curves from grim-reaper chains

section: 5.7 Immersed ancient curves from grim-reaper chains
text: 104CF0DAFD60 Angenent–You construct compact and noncompact immersed ancient curve-shortening flows from ordered chains of grim reapers. Consecutive horizontal asymptotes $y=a_{k-1},a_ k$, with distinct adjacent heights, determine the grim speed $v_ k=\pi /|a_ k-a_{k-1}|$ and the direction is chosen as in their formula (3). The complete cyclic closing and intersection requirements in Sections 2–4 are essential; arbitrary superposition is not a solution. The compact case has a closing grim arc and parameter domain $S^1$. The noncompact construction has parameter domain $\mathbb R$, two ends asymptotic to the first and last horizontal lines, and the parity condition in the source. The construction includes locally convex immersed curves and curves that are neither embedded nor locally convex. These are distinct from the previously recorded embedded eternal chain examples. Their time interval is $(-\infty ,T)$ for some endpoint $T$, with no general eternal continuation claim for the compact case. The figure shows the limiting grim pieces and connections at several increasingly late schematic stages. The finite-time gluing correction is not computed, and crossings in the intended planar immersed example are distinguished from artifacts of a higher-dimensional projection. text:
Numerical references This page credits the numerical methods, software, and visual sources used to make the figures in MCF-stack. The mathematical existence and classification references remain with each example and in the bibliography . A newly generated mesh or rendering can still owe its visual conception to another author's picture. Visual sources Drawing methods Methods and software references Code and provenance Visual sources and individual credits The credits below identify documented visual influences and parametrization sources. Where a paper credits an individual illustrator, that credit is retained separately from the paper's authorship. Newly generated schematic geometry is not the source author's numerical mesh. Höskuldur P. Halldórsson The planar classification , Sections 2–5 and Figures 4–19, supplies the ODEs and visual references for the annulus-dense shrinkers, rotators, expanding spirals and rotating shrinking spirals. The helicoidal paper , equations (3.3), (4.1) and (5.3), and Figures 1–4, supplies the helicoidal translator ODE and the classical minimal-surface formula attributed there to Wunderlich. All displayed geometry is newly generated by scripts/generate_halldorsson_geometry.py ; no paper figures or source meshes are redistributed. SciPy DOP853 integrates the arclength systems. A scalar Brent solve targets the irrational turning condition; finite precision does not certify irrationality. A comet preset uses finite-radius asymptotic shooting and is explicitly an approximation to the special orbit. Refinement and equation diagnostics are recorded in the geometry audit , without rigorous error bounds. Minimal helicoids are sampled from the exact formula. The viewers apply exact similarity motions to finite patches, and use equal spatial scales. Dashed circles mark accumulation sets, not extra flow components. David L. Chopp Chopp's Computation of Self-Similar Solutions for Mean Curvature Flow , Experimental Mathematics 3 (1994), 1–15 supplies the numerical candidates and visual references for the five Chopp entries: Figures 8–12 (cubical), 13–15 (octahedral), 16–19 (saddle), 20–23 (two-handled cone), and 26–28 (four-handled cone). The latter also appears in Angenent–Ilmanen–Chopp, A Computed Example of Nonuniqueness of Mean Curvature Flow in R3 (1995), p. 1943 . Chopp is also credited for Figure 1 in Ilmanen–White, Fattening in Mean Curvature Flow , which informs our two-ended topology drawing, and Figure 2 in Hoffman–Martín–White , a visual reference for the cubical silhouette. Our corresponding models are schematics, not recomputations of Chopp's numerical surfaces. Source review and drawing provenance . Tom Ilmanen The conjectural genus-eight picture credited to Ilmanen in Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller, Mean curvature self-shrinkers of high genus: Non-compact examples , Figure 1 , is a visual reference for the sphere–plane configuration. Our KKM drawing uses the paper's Scherk equation and a project-specific drawing map; it is not a solved shrinker or the paper's matched initial surface. Drawing provenance . O. Michael Melko Melko's Visualizing Minimal Surfaces (2010), equations (16)–(19) , provides the stationary Costa parametrization used for the ancient-Costa illustration. The project evaluates this parametrization and adds a truncated linearized normal mode. Those perturbed frames are not a numerical construction of the nonlinear ancient flow. Implementation and limitations . Su–Tsai–Wood: infinite-time Lagrangian neck collapse The signed-profile time plate and interactive comparison are newly drawn from Su, Tsai and Wood, Infinite-Time Singularities of the Lagrangian Mean Curvature Flow : Section 2.3 gives the Lawlor neck, equation (1.1) gives its leading-order scale dynamics, and Proposition 9.5 identifies the rescaled limit. Figures 1–2 explain the desingularization and compact topology. No paper figure or mesh is copied. The local equal-angle profiles are exact; the time-dependent scaling and global topology diagram illustrate the construction and do not compute the compact flow. Formulas, scope, and reproducibility . Lee–Wang quadric flow The shrinker time plate and circle-action viewer are original drawings from Lee and Wang, Hamiltonian stationary cones and self-similar solutions in higher dimension , Theorem 1.1 and Sections 2–3. They sample the exact unit-weight coordinates in C³; no PDE is solved. The displayed phase leaves and projected orbit curves are labeled as such. The SVG and browser canvas use the same coordinate generator, with a fixed ambient crop and scale across times. No figure, mesh, or software from the paper is reproduced. The companion expander illustration samples the exact real slices x₃ = ±√(x₁² + x₂² + 2t) at positive times and the singular cone at t = 0. The comparison keeps one spatial scale and a fixed radial display cutoff. Its circle-orbit diagram is drawn in the exact two-plane spanned by x and i(x₁,x₂,−x₃) in R⁶; changing the circle phase keeps flow time fixed. These real slices are not themselves mean curvature flows in R³. See the expander geometry and verification notes . Mario B. Schulz The illustration for the work of Reto Buzano, Huy The Nguyen, and Mario B. Schulz follows the qualitative geometry of Section 4, Figures 3–4 of Noncompact self-shrinkers for mean curvature flow with arbitrary genus , version 2 . These are visual references as well as mathematical source material. The authors produced their simulations with Kenneth Brakke's Surface Evolver . Our mesh instead samples an illustrative implicit field. BNS drawing provenance . Schulz is individually credited for Figure 5, the genus-five numerical picture in Hoffman–Martín–White, Generating Shrinkers by Mean Curvature Flow , version 3 . It informs our sphere–plane drawing and its interior view, together with Torralbo's figures below. Schulz's Geometric Analysis Gallery , especially its self-shrinker collection , is an additional resource for these visualizations. The documented sources used for our drawings are the paper figures identified above; the gallery link does not assert that the website itself was consulted during the original implementation, or that its images or meshes were reused. Ao Sun: supplied Chu–Sun numerical replay pages The two supplementary Chu–Sun experiment viewers were supplied by Ao Sun with their numerical-note and archive provenance retained. Both use three.js 0.128.0 ; the first also uses pako 2.1.0 to decompress stored frames. These are replays of supplied computations, not numerical experiments independently reproduced by the website integration. See the integration and provenance record and the retained three.js and pako license notices. Private notes and solver archives are not exported. Francisco Torralbo Torralbo is credited for the numerical genus-one through genus-six illustrations in Hoffman–Martín–White, Figure 1 . They inform the qualitative appearance of our sphere–plane model, alongside Schulz's Figure 5. The displayed MCF-stack surface is a topology schematic. Sphere–plane drawing provenance . Matthias Weber Weber is credited for Hoffman–Martín–White, Figure 7 , a visual reference for our three-ended model. The source describes a conjectural qualitative genus-two picture, not a numerical shrinker approximation. Our separately generated mesh retains that distinction. Three-ended drawing provenance . Other source-specific drawing references Other figures use the source paper's profiles or construction diagrams. Examples include Drugan's Figure 1, Møller's Figures 1–2, Nguyen's Figure 1, and the planar-network diagrams reviewed for the expander picture. Their exact roles are recorded in the Drugan , Møller , Nguyen , and network provenance notes. The figure documentation supplies further source locators; this page does not replace the individual example references. Drawing methods and their scope Formula sampling and projection. Parametrizations are sampled into curves or triangles. Revolving a profile, taking a slice, or projecting from a higher-dimensional ambient space is identified in the caption. The mesh is a finite representation of the formula. Numerical ODE profiles. SciPy integration and, where required, Brent root finding produce profiles with closing or matching conditions. DOP853 is used in several generators. The interactive Abresch–Langer viewer also has a custom period quadrature and bisection implementation. Solver settings and residuals are recorded in the relevant code and audit. Numerical PDE and flow models. Selected generators use finite differences, sparse linear solves, or truncated linearized evolution. Their specific discretizations and limitations accompany the figures. A finite-domain calculation or linearized perturbation is not automatically a computed complete soliton or nonlinear ancient flow. Implicit schematic meshes. Marching cubes extracts a surface from a sampled drawing field; quadric simplification reduces its triangle count. Connectivity, boundary loops, and Euler characteristic are checked where recorded. These checks describe the displayed mesh and do not establish the shrinker equation. Rendering. Custom Python and JavaScript code produces SVG plates and Canvas/WebGL viewers with projection, shading, rotation, zoom, and cutaways. The supplied Chu–Sun replay pages additionally use three.js. Pillow supplies raster panels in selected plates; trimesh supplies selected mesh operations. Cutaway edges and finite display rims are explained in the captions.
